Relational or document stores where a coarse-grained business object is composed of finer-grained dependent objects whose lifecycle is bound to it. Applies when clients - especially remote ones - should exchange one coarse-grained structure instead of the parts, when the persist/synchronise boundary must coincide with one transaction, and when each dependent can still own its own mapping. Modern form: an aggregate root mapped with cascading associations or with components stored in the root's own row.
Order with line items, shipment addresses and payment allocations that must be written and deleted as one business unit.
Customer or account aggregate holding addresses, contact methods and preferences that are edited in one form and saved once.
Document-style clusters (invoice with revisions, article with embedded sections) where the parts only exist inside the root.
Legacy-style coarse-grained entity beans that wrap fine-grained POJOs so that clients exchange one composite transfer object instead of many fine-grained ones.
Mobile or remote clients that must send one coarse-grained payload per edit instead of a sequence of dependent calls.
Batch imports where a cluster is validated and written transactionally, so a partially imported entity never exists.
DDD Bounded Contexts where one aggregate encapsulates a complete business invariant enforced across multiple related entities — e.g., a Rental aggregate containing a rental agreement, reserved vehicle, and driver assignment that must all be created or fail together.
CQRS write models where the aggregate is the sole write target and all state changes flow through the root's command methods, ensuring every mutation is a coherent cluster-level operation.
Event sourcing snapshots where the aggregate root serialises its entire graph so that snapshot restore reconstructs the full composite in one operation rather than re-playing individual dependent events.
Legacy system facades that wrap a network of fine-grained remote beans behind a single coarse-grained composite interface, collapsing many remote calls into one round-trip for external clients.
SQLAlchemy parent-child clusters mapped with cascade='all, delete-orphan' on relationship(): disassociating a child deletes the row, so the Session flushes the cluster as one unit without per-child Session.delete() calls.
EF Core owned types: dependent types stored in the owner's table (or as owned navigations) share the aggregate root's identity and save with a single context.SaveChanges().
Mongoose subdocument arrays: embedded parts are saved, validated and removed through the top-level document, so the cluster's lifecycle is bound to the root document's save.

poison-pill
sentinel message
end-of-stream marker
Terminate queue consumers cooperatively by sending a reserved sentinel message that each consumer recognises as "no more work", so consumers drain the backlog and exit without a separate control channel or forced cancellation.
A producer-consumer system must shut down, but its consumers block on an empty queue and the queue has no built-in "no more items" signal: callers either kill the workers mid-work and drop buffered items, or leave them blocked forever. Production has ended - how do the consumers learn that while still processing everything already queued?
In-process or broker-mediated producer-consumer systems with a FIFO work queue, a fixed set of long-lived consumers (threads, coroutines, actors) that block when the queue is empty, and a shutdown requirement that work already accepted by the queue be drained before the consumers exit - typically deployment, signal handling or test teardown.
Signal-driven shutdown of an in-process worker pool: the SIGTERM handler stops accepting work, then enqueues one pill per worker so the backlog is processed before the process exits.
Batch importers and ETL stages whose consumers block on a work queue and must finish the current batch before a run is considered complete.
Test harnesses and simulations: an explicit stop message makes thread-based systems deterministic to shut down, without sleeps or guessed timeouts.
Actor systems: a reserved stop message (for example Akka PoisonPill) terminates an actor after the messages already queued for it have been handled.
Log and event writers where the last records must reach the sink before consumers release their buffers and files.
Bounded-queue stages in a pipeline: pills travel the same backpressured channel as work, so upstream cannot keep producing after the stop decision.
Kubernetes pod shutdown: containers receive SIGTERM, workers stop pulling from the job queue, drain in-flight tasks, then exit within the terminationGracePeriodSeconds window.
Redis/Bull queue workers: a shutdown signal pushes a sentinel via BLPOP so workers exit cleanly without losing the right to process pending tasks.
Akka Streams and similar streaming frameworks: the GraphStage signals completion via onPull/downstream cancellation, which is the materialised equivalent of a poison pill.
Redis Streams consumer groups: XREADGROUP with block timeout naturally returns when the stream is empty; a special ID (e.g. ">") polling loop plus a shared shutdown flag replaces the in-process sentinel.
Broker-level poison message isolation: in Kafka, RabbitMQ, or Azure Service Bus, a permanently failing message (deserialisation error, validation failure) blocks a partition/consumer indefinitely; DLQ-based routing (publish to dead-letter topic after N retries, then commit offset and continue) is the broker-level analogue that prevents one poison message from halting the entire pipeline.
Kubernetes preStop hooks + pill drain: a container's lifecycle preStop hook can enqueue a sentinel into an in-process work queue while the orchestrator grants terminationGracePeriodSeconds for the drain to complete, ensuring zero work-drop during rolling updates.
Azure Service Bus competing-consumers workers: when a worker receives a shutdown notification it completes its current PeekLock message, then calls Abandon on any held locks before unregistering; Azure Service Bus dead-letter queues handle the poison-message variant when a message exceeds MaxDeliveryCount and cannot be delivered.
Akka hierarchical actor trees: sending PoisonPill to a parent actor stops it after all queued messages ahead of the pill are processed, and automatically sends stop messages to all children in bottom-up order; this is the idiomatic way to orchestrate ordered multi-actor shutdown.
Non-blocking retry architectures (RabbitMQ): rather than local Thread.sleep retries that block the consumer thread, use server-side TTL queues with Dead Letter Exchange routing to implement exponential backoff, keeping the consumer responsive to new messages and to shutdown pills.
Java's JDK BlockingQueue worker pools: because BlockingQueue has no built-in close, producers can enqueue a unique end-of-stream object after all work; each consumer takes until that sentinel and then the coordinator joins workers.
Python multiprocessing worker pools: multiprocessing.Queue/JoinableQueue supports FIFO task delivery with sentinel values and join-based drain tracking; send one sentinel per worker and join them after the queue is exhausted.
Akka Classic actors: PoisonPill is enqueued in the mailbox and processed after already queued messages, while Akka Typed requires an explicit Stop/Shutdown protocol; choose the API that matches the actor model.

recursive-descent-parser
recursive descent
recursive descent parsing
Parse a small grammar by translating every rule directly into a function that consumes the tokens the rule matches and calls the functions of the rules it references, so the parser's control flow is the grammar itself and stays readable, debuggable and free of a code-generation step.
A hand-written parser is the only option - no generator in the toolchain, or the grammar is a small DSL - yet the grammar is not a flat token sequence: alternatives must be chosen from lookahead, repetition must become a loop, and the natural grammar for expressions is left-recursive, which a top-down parser cannot translate directly. Without a disciplined mapping from rules to functions the parser degenerates into ad-hoc index arithmetic and exception-driven backtracking, and errors end up without positions.
Front ends for small languages, DSLs, query/filter/rule grammars, configuration and protocol formats, and the parsing layer of compilers and interpreters that want no code-generation step. It applies when a lexer or token stream already exists (or is cheap to write), the grammar is small to medium and reasonably LL-friendly or rewritable into LL form, and the team values readable, step-debuggable, position-precise parsing over generated tables.
Front ends for small languages, DSLs and configuration formats (filter expressions, rule engines, policy languages, template syntaxes) where a generator and its build integration would be overkill.
Expression and statement parsing in single-pass compilers and interpreters that emit bytecode or IR while parsing, as in Crafting Interpreters' Lox.
Tooling for a grammar you own - formatters, linters, syntax highlighters, language servers - where error tolerance, multiple diagnostics and exact positions matter more than raw throughput.
Protocol and wire-format decoding with a small fixed grammar, where errors must carry byte offsets and malformed input must be rejected deterministically.
Context-dependent or indentation-sensitive syntaxes (templates with interpolation, layout-based blocks, configuration with embedded expressions) that a generated lexer handles poorly.
Codebases that must not carry generated code: security-reviewed, vendored or cross-compiled projects where an ordinary source file beats a build-time generator.
Clang's C-family front end uses a unified hand-built recursive-descent parser for C, C++, Objective-C and Objective-C++, pairing rule-oriented control flow with production-quality diagnostics.
The Go standard library's go/parser is a production recursive-descent parser for Go source, with explicit parser state, nesting-depth guards and error recovery.
rustc_parse is the Rust compiler's recursive-descent parser module, showing how a hand-written parser can scale to macros, recovery modes and detailed token/state handling.
Lua's reference implementation compiles with lparser.c, a single-pass recursive-descent parser that emits bytecode opcodes while reducing expressions instead of building a syntax tree, with precedence handled by parsing levels.

event-aggregator
event bus
messenger
message bus
event hub
Funnel the events of many source objects into one hub that owns the subscription wiring, so that subscribers register once with the aggregator instead of tracking down and registering with every publisher.
Many components raise events and many components want to react: if every consumer registers directly with every producer, each consumer has to find the sources and subscribe to each event type separately, each producer accumulates knowledge of who listens, and both sides repeat the same registration and unsubscribe code at every pair. The trigger is a many-publisher / many-subscriber setting in which the wiring itself has become the maintenance problem.
In-process, event-driven software - a modular UI shell, a domain-event pipeline inside one bounded context, a plugin host, a simulation or instrumentation layer - where publishers and subscribers grow independently, both sides should stay unaware of each other, and registration plus lifetime management should live in one place. The aggregator is a component- or module-scope element of one process (one node); events that must cross a process boundary, survive a restart or be delivered reliably need a messaging channel instead.
Modular UI shells (WPF/MAUI, Android, SwiftUI) where view models living in separate modules must react to each other without holding references — the classic Prism and CommunityToolkit.Mvvm scenario.
Domain-event fan-out inside one bounded context: 'order placed' reaches billing, stock, notification and audit services that each subscribe to the hub instead of to the Order aggregate.
Plugin, extension or rule hosts where the listener set is only known at runtime and plugins are loaded and unloaded while the application runs.
Test and simulation harnesses: a test subscribes to the hub, drives one publisher and asserts on the published events without wiring up the real consumers.
Cross-cutting instrumentation and audit: metrics, tracing, logging and audit collectors receive events from many components through one hub rather than being called from each component.
Long-running services broadcasting rare state changes (configuration reload, presence change, feature-flag flip) to every interested subsystem exactly once per change.
Micro-frontend communication: independent web apps in one page communicating via a shared event bus with typed event maps and cross-tab synchronization (BroadcastChannel bridge).
IoT sensor aggregation: many sensor streams funnelled through one hub for filtering, transformation and fan-out to display or downstream processing services.
CQRS command/event pipeline: commands are dispatched to handlers that publish domain events through a bus; read-model projectors subscribe to build consistent query views.
Redux/Flux-style frontend state updates where UI components subscribe to dispatched actions rather than mutating shared state directly.
Event storm prevention harness: wrapping a batch save operation in a scoped subscriber-disable guard so that handlers triggered by the save do not re-publish events that would cascade back through the same handler.
Transactional outbox companion: publishing domain events through the hub after a transaction commits, ensuring that state changes and event emission are not separated by a process crash (in-process equivalent of the outbox pattern).
Java in-JVM decoupling with Guava EventBus: objects register via @Subscribe-annotated methods and publishers post typed events that the bus routes by parameter type (superclasses and interfaces included), with unmatched events wrapped as DeadEvent for a second-chance subscriber.
Spring application-context event pipeline: beans publish through ApplicationEventPublisher and react via @EventListener methods - in-process domain-event fan-out with the ApplicationEventMulticaster owning the registry, no message broker involved.
Vue 2 cross-component communication through a shared root instance used as a global bus ($on/$emit); Vue 3 removed that instance-emitter API, making external typed emitters like mitt, provide/inject, or a store (Pinia) the supported replacement - a cautionary real-world case for untyped global buses.

converter
translator
Give a pair of corresponding representations one owner that maps them into each other in both directions, so every caller converts through one place and neither representation has to import, know or be aware of the other.
The same information lives in two representations - domain object and DTO, in-memory value and wire or column format, internal model and third-party schema - and both directions are exercised in production. Hand-written field copying at each call site duplicates the mapping rules, drifts whenever either representation changes, and forces at least one side (or every caller) to import the other.
Component boundaries where an internal model meets an external representation: service or API layers exchanging DTOs, persistence layers mapping values to column formats, integration seams facing a third-party or legacy schema, and codec layers mapping typed values to a wire format. It applies whenever both directions are needed (read and write, decode and encode) and either side must stay independent of the other - different modules, teams, release cycles or libraries.
Domain object <-> DTO at a service or API boundary, where the transport shape must not leak into the model.
Value object <-> database column representation (JPA AttributeConverter, EF Core ValueConverter, Rails custom attribute type).
Third-party or legacy schema <-> internal model at an integration seam, including versioned wire formats.
Typed value <-> JSON, XML or protobuf payload with a custom codec when the default mapping is wrong (formats, units, enums).
Query rows or record sets <-> domain objects, where a full mapper framework would be oversized.
Single-value wrappers such as identifiers, money or unit-carrying quantities mapped to and from their primitive form.
Palindrome conversion chain (Entity -> DAO -> DTO -> Controller -> DTO -> DAO -> Entity) where each layer owns exactly one transformation direction, making the data flow explicit and each boundary independently testable.
Versioned API contracts: a DTO for API v1 and a separate DTO for API v2 coexist; a converter pair maps each version's DTO to the shared internal model, isolating API consumers from internal changes.
API gateway transformation: external third-party API payloads are normalized into an internal canonical format at the gateway, and outbound responses are converted back to the third-party schema; converters live at the seam.
Event-driven payload normalization: domain events carry one representation (e.g., enriched entity) while the event bus transports a flattened wire format (e.g., protobuf); converters at producer and consumer ends keep the two shapes in sync.
ORM entity vs. read-model DTO at the query boundary: a repository executes a query and the row-set converter maps each row to a read-model DTO, avoiding the entity in read-only paths entirely.
Anti-corruption layer at legacy integration seams: external system payloads are translated into the internal domain model at the boundary, and responses translated back; the converter owns the translation vocabulary, protecting the domain model from foreign concepts (Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design; Microsoft Azure Architecture Center; AWS Prescriptive Guidance).
Immutable value type <-> wire format for cryptographic or financial domains: the converter is a lawful isomorphism ensuring every wire value round-trips to an identical object (tested via property-based round-trip laws, as in the lawful-conversions Haskell library and Higher-Kinded-J Iso optics library).
Strangler-fig migration seam: new microservice functionality is accessed through an ACL that converts legacy system payloads to the new domain model and back, keeping the legacy interface unchanged while the new service evolves behind the seam.
Guava com.google.common.base.Converter<F, T>: an abstract bidirectional function with convert()/reverse(), automatic reverse() derivation for subclasses, mapAll() for whole iterables and Converter.normalize() to lift a converter into a function converter - the pattern as a shipped JDK-adjacent library type (Google Guava).
Go database/sql custom types: a type implementing both sql.Scanner (Scan(src any) error) and driver.Valuer (Value() (driver.Value, error)) owns the Go value <-> database column pair in both directions; the standard library's NullString, NullInt64 and NullTime are built-in pairs of exactly this shape.
Rails custom attribute types: subclass ActiveModel::Type::Value, override serialize (Ruby value -> database value) and deserialize (database value -> Ruby value) and bind with attribute :col, MyType.new - the converter pair at the ORM seam, with cast_value kept separate for user-input coercion.

monitor-object
thread-safe passive object
monitor
Serialise concurrent method invocations on a shared object by giving the object its own lock and condition variables, so that only one method executes inside it at a time and methods that cannot proceed wait cooperatively instead of polling.
Objects shared by several threads expose their state through ordinary methods, and nothing stops concurrent callers from interleaving inside those methods, corrupting the invariants they were written to maintain. The race is then papered over with ad-hoc locking, sleeps and busy-wait loops scattered through client code. The recurring decision is whether the object itself should own the serialisation (and the scheduling) of its methods instead of leaving that discipline to every caller.
Shared-memory concurrency, where the mutable state of an object is reached by more than one thread and its methods must be atomic with respect to one another. It matters most when some methods cannot run to completion until another method changes the state - a queue that is full or empty, a resource that is not yet available, a phase that has not been reached - because then a method must suspend and later resume, which requires releasing the lock while it waits.
Bounded buffers and work queues shared by producer and consumer threads, where producers wait while the queue is full and consumers wait while it is empty - the pattern's canonical example.
Session, connection or entity registries on a server, where lookups, insertion and eviction must be atomic and callers may have to wait for capacity or for an entry to reappear.
Caches with in-flight bookkeeping (single-flight computation), where a thread that requests an already-computed key waits for the first thread's result instead of recomputing it.
Shared configuration, counters or statistics objects read and updated by request threads, where each call must observe a consistent snapshot of the state.
State machines and simulators whose step methods block until another thread advances a transition, for example a test harness waiting for a worker to reach a known state.
In-process resource pools (connection, database or worker pools) where acquisition blocks until an entry is returned or a timeout expires.
Java's java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue is a fixed-capacity monitor-style bounded buffer: put blocks while full and take blocks while empty, making the producer-consumer coordination explicit.
.NET's System.Collections.Concurrent.BlockingCollection<T> supplies bounded Add/Take blocking, cancellation and completion semantics around a producer-consumer collection; use it instead of hand-rolling Monitor.Wait/Pulse.
Python's queue.Queue provides a thread-safe multi-producer/multi-consumer boundary with blocking put/get operations and optional timeouts, a standard monitor-style primitive for worker pools.

double-dispatch
multiple dispatch
multiple polymorphism
two-level dispatch
Select the operation to execute from the runtime types of two collaborating objects, so behaviour can vary along two independent type axes instead of being resolved by hand-written type tests in the caller.
Behaviour depends on the runtime type of *two* objects - element and visitor, shape and surface, left operand and right operand - but an ordinary call resolves on the receiver only (or, in dynamic languages, on no argument at all). Every operation then grows its own type-test ladder, knowledge of the concrete classes leaks into callers, and adding a class silently breaks the cases nobody remembered to extend.
Object models in which two type hierarchies interact: shape x medium, AST node x operation, operand x operand, entity x entity in a collision matrix. It applies when the pair-specific behaviour is a real matrix rather than a single special case, when each hierarchy evolves on its own schedule, and when the language's own dispatch resolves only one of the two runtime types (classic single-dispatch OO) or none of them (method overloading is bound statically).
Collision and interaction rules in games and simulations: every pair of entity types (bullet × wall, ship × asteroid) has its own outcome. Double dispatch cleanly selects the correct collision algorithm at runtime. Used in Unity, Unreal, and custom game engines via visitor-like hierarchies or type-indexed collision matrices. Spatial partitioning (quad-trees, oct-trees) is used alongside to reduce O(n²) pair checks. Examples: Unity physics collision callbacks, Unreal collision/overlap event system, Box2D physics engine, custom engines with AABB/Sphere/OBB hierarchies.
Geometry predicates between two shape hierarchies: intersect, contains, distance and other predicates where each pair (circle-circle, circle-rectangle, rectangle-rectangle) uses a different algorithm and pairs are not symmetric. Used in game physics engines, computer graphics rendering pipelines, and GIS systems. Examples: Box2D, Chipmunk, computer graphics rendering engines.
Numeric promotion and operator semantics between unrelated numeric types: Rational × Integer, Money × Currency, BigInt × Float — operations that must consult both operands' concrete types. Ruby's Numeric#coerce is the canonical language mechanism enabling this pattern. Examples: Ruby Numeric#coerce, Java BigDecimal arithmetic, C# decimal/float/double mixed arithmetic.
Document rendering and media output: shapes or widgets × output targets (screen, printer, PDF, HTML), where each combination emits different code. The medium axis and the shape type axis independently determine the rendering path. Examples: Qt/wxWidgets painting systems, Java AWT/Swing paint(Graphics) dispatch, WebKit/Blink layout engines.
AST traversal and transformations: one node hierarchy × many analyses (type check, pretty-print, evaluate, optimise) — the primary use case the Visitor pattern was designed for. Each (Operation × NodeType) pair is a separate handler. Examples: Babel/TypeScript compiler, LLVM compiler infrastructure, Roslyn C# compiler API.
Plugin and extension architectures: a host application defines an element hierarchy and a plugin defines a visitor; new plugins add operations without modifying element classes. Examples: Eclipse IDE plugin system, Visual Studio Analyzer/extension APIs, static analysis tools (linters, formatters).
Serialization and deserialization frameworks: Format (JSON, XML, binary, protobuf) × type — each combination may need different encoding rules. Examples: Jackson/Gson in Java, Python dataclasses serialization, Protocol Buffers schema evolution.
Protocol handling in parsers and state machines: handler depends on both message kind and connection/session kind — a state × event matrix. Used in network protocol stacks, parsers, and finite state machine implementations. Examples: HTTP server request routing, game AI state machines, telecom protocol state tables.
Event handling in GUI frameworks: a widget hierarchy × an event hierarchy (mouse, keyboard, focus) — each (Widget × Event) pair may require different handling logic. The classic AWT/Swing processEvent double-dispatch was the motivating example for several academic multi-dispatch papers. Examples: Java AWT event delegation, Qt event handling, Swing ActionMap/InputMap.
Message routing in game architectures: entity × message type routing where the correct handler depends on both the receiver entity's type and the message's payload type. Common in Entity-Component-System (ECS) patterns where components process messages differently. Examples: Unity MessageSystem, Amazon Lumberyard (component × message routing).
Numeric and array operators as native multiple dispatch: Julia makes the pair axis first-class - arithmetic and promotion operators are generic functions whose methods select on the runtime types of all arguments, and the compiler emits a specialised version per concrete combination (Int,Int vs Float64,Float64) instead of a hand-rolled accept/visit round-trip; promote_type absorbs cross-type cells. The canonical modern realisation of the pattern. Examples: Julia Base arithmetic, Julia promote_type/coercion, heterogeneous-array dispatch costs documented in the Julia performance guide.
Generic functions in CLOS and Dylan-family languages: method selection keyed by the classes or identities of every required argument, with method combination (call-next-method) resolving ambiguity - double dispatch without the intrusive accept method, and the benchmark every manual encoding is measured against. Examples: ANSI Common Lisp CLOS defgeneric/defmethod, Dylan generic functions.
Runtime binder dispatch on the CLR: the C# dynamic keyword defers overload resolution to the Dynamic Language Runtime, binding the call on the runtime types of receiver and arguments with call-site caching; CallSiteBinder.Bind is documented as runtime binding (double-dispatch). A missing pair surfaces as a runtime binder exception rather than a compile error, so it suits dynamic-language and COM interop boundaries more than closed business matrices. Examples: DLR call-site caching, IronPython/IronRuby interop, COM interop via the runtime binder.

identity-map
first-level cache
session cache
Guarantee that within one session every database row is represented by exactly one in-memory object, by keeping a keyed registry of loaded objects that every load consults before hitting the database.
Two code paths in the same session load the same row into two different objects: updates through one are invisible to the other, the last flush silently wins, and every load pays the remote-call cost again. The catalog states the invariant as: the same row must never be two different in-memory objects in one session.
Object-oriented persistence (data mappers, repositories, unit of work) where entities carry a stable database identity (an Identity Field) and several parts of one business transaction or request refer to the same rows. Applies whenever duplicate in-memory instances would break graph consistency or lose updates - typically inside an ORM session or a hand-written persistence context whose lifetime bounds staleness.
ORM sessions in web request handling (JPA EntityManager, EF Core DbContext, SQLAlchemy Session, MikroORM EntityManager) where several services touch the same entities in one request.
Batch import and synchronisation jobs that re-read the same rows repeatedly inside one transaction and must not operate on divergent copies.
Object graph reconstruction in data mappers, where cycles and shared references need one in-memory instance per row.
Desktop and document applications with a context-scoped object space (Core Data contexts) where objects are edited, undone and saved as one unit.
Hand-written persistence layers over plain SQL where two repositories serve the same table and must agree on identity.
CQRS command handlers where the same aggregate is loaded multiple times within one command execution — the identity map prevents duplicate instances from forming across repository calls within the same session.
Event-sourced aggregate reconstruction: replaying events to rebuild aggregate state requires the same aggregate instance to accumulate state across multiple event applications; identity map guarantees a single instance per aggregate ID per reconstruction session.
Microservices saga and choreography: within one service's unit-of-work, multiple steps may load the same entity; identity map ensures all steps operate on the same instance even when the entity is referenced across different event handlers.
DDD bounded-context integration: when one bounded context holds a reference to an entity from another context (by ID), that entity is resolved through the local identity map — multiple resolution paths must all consult the same map to stay consistent.
Testing scenarios where the same entity is accessed via multiple repository paths: identity map guarantees test assertions see the same instance regardless of which repository method returned it, enabling meaningful state verification.
Multi-tenant applications where each tenant request gets its own session/identity-map scope, preventing cross-tenant data leakage by construction — a shared/global map would allow one tenant's rows to shadow another's.
SQLAlchemy Session.get in a unit of work: repeated primary-key loads return the same Python object from the Session identity map, while the Session is deliberately not a cross-session query cache.
EF Core tracked queries and AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution: the DbContext keeps one entity instance per key for tracked results, while no-tracking identity resolution is opt-in for read models.
Hibernate Session persistence contexts: repeated loads of the same entity type and identifier resolve to the one managed instance per Session, so entity graphs and dirty checking share state.

range
interval
Represent a span of values as a single interval value whose bound inclusivity and open ends are explicit, so containment and interval-to-interval comparisons live in one place instead of repeated ad-hoc endpoint tests.
Start and end travel together through the code but every caller re-derives what they mean: containment is written as scattered <= / < comparisons that drift apart, "unbounded" is smuggled in as a sentinel value (Long.MAX_VALUE, 9999-12-31), and interval-to-interval questions - do these two overlap, does one enclose the other, what is the gap between them - have no home at all.
Applies wherever a domain concept is a span rather than a point: validity and effectivity periods, booking and availability windows, quantity or price tiers, measurement buckets, version and address ranges, pagination windows, and query parameters such as a date range. It pays off when the same interval is compared repeatedly or crosses a boundary (persistence, API payloads, UI widgets), because the bound convention then has to be written once instead of re-decided per call site. For a single comparison between two local variables the type is pure overhead.
Validity and effectivity windows: a contract, price or membership is valid over [effectiveFrom, effectiveTo), and every check is a membership test against one interval.
Booking and availability: a room, seat or resource is reserved during an interval; overlap (not adjacency) decides whether a new booking is possible, and back-to-back bookings must be allowed deliberately.
Quantity and price tiers: the unit price depends on the quantity interval ([1,10), [10,50), [50, +inf)), so a container of intervals with containment lookup replaces a cascade of if-statements.
Temporal queries and reporting: "last 7 days", "this quarter", "since the migration" are half-open or open-ended intervals passed to repositories and rendered by date-range pickers.
Version, port and address ranges: a compatibility claim covers [1.2, 2.0) of a library, a firewall rule covers a port interval - containment answers "is this covered?" and intersection answers "do these rules conflict?".
Pagination and slicing windows: a page is an interval over a sequence, and half-open semantics make adjacency exact ([0,20) followed by [20,40)),
PostgreSQL range and multirange columns: PostgreSQL's daterange, tsrange and numeric range types make lower-inclusive/upper-exclusive bounds, overlap and containment operators, and indexed range queries part of the persistence contract; choose the bound convention before mapping domain intervals.
Guava Range: Java's Guava Range models convex bounded or unbounded intervals with nine open/closed forms, isConnected and intersection; use ContiguousSet only when a discrete domain really requires enumeration rather than treating the interval itself as a sequence.
Standard-library and container choices: Rust's std::ops::RangeBounds covers included, excluded and unbounded bounds when its range forms fit; for many intervals requiring join/split policies, Boost ICL's interval_set and interval_map supply the container semantics instead of overloading one Range value.

bulkhead
bulkhead isolation
cell-based architecture
Partition finite shared capacity at the failure domain (dependency, tenant, priority class, or cell) into independently bounded pools or permits, with an explicit queue and saturation policy, so one slow, saturated, or failing participant cannot consume capacity reserved for others.
Several dependencies or tenants share thread, connection, worker, or permit pools. When one becomes slow, leaky, or overloaded, its calls hold shared slots and fill shared queues, so unrelated work queues and fails behind it; the design needs a boundary that contains resource exhaustion without pretending to isolate CPU, network, or server-side limits that remain shared.
Any component whose concurrency is a finite resource: a service calling multiple downstream APIs, a multi-tenant workload, a job runner mixing interactive and batch work, or an inference and gateway tier with per-deployment quotas. The failure mode to contain is degradation and overload (slow dependency, connection leak, traffic spike), not only hard failure, and the isolation boundary must be chosen at the failure domain - instance, dependency, tenant or priority class.
A service that calls several downstream APIs through one shared HTTP client: give each downstream its own connection and thread budget so one hanging endpoint cannot block the others.
Multi-tenant SaaS where one tenant's workload must not consume the concurrency available to other tenants (per-tenant pools).
Interactive request traffic sharing a database with batch or report jobs: separate pools per workload class keep the database from serialising everything behind the batch.
An API gateway or backend-for-frontend routing to many backends with per-route concurrency caps, so a slow backend does not consume the proxy's shared capacity.
Job workers that mix latency-critical and background queues: per-queue worker pools prevent a backlog of background jobs from starving urgent work.
Inference and AI serving where each model deployment has its own concurrency quota and a saturated model must not consume the shared request capacity.
Cell-based architectures: each cell (complete, independent service instance) is a bulkhead partition; load grows by adding cells, and a failure is contained to the single cell — used at AWS, Google, and Netflix scale.
Shuffle sharding: Amazon Route 53-style virtual shard assignment where each tenant is assigned to a random shard of two or more cells; with eight cells and two-per-shard there are 28 unique shards, so a problem affects only 1/28th of tenants — far better than regular per-cell partitioning.
AI and inference workloads: per-deployment or per-tenant Azure OpenAI or LLM deployment quotas prevent one saturated model from consuming the shared request capacity across the platform.
Database RU isolation: Azure Cosmos DB request-unit throughput assigned per container acts as a storage-layer bulkhead; one noisy container cannot exhaust the RU budget of others.
Resilience4j's SemaphoreBulkhead and FixedThreadPoolBulkhead give a JVM service per-dependency permits versus a bounded queue and worker pool; choose based on whether caller threads may be occupied.
Netflix Hystrix's per-command thread pools or semaphore isolation reject work and route it to fallback, containing a slow downstream to its command boundary (historical and deprecated).
.NET services use Polly's BulkheadPolicy/AsyncBulkheadPolicy (maxParallelization plus maxQueuingActions, rejecting with BulkheadRejectedException when both are full); Polly v8 replaced it with ConcurrencyLimiter over System.Threading.RateLimiting, whose partitioned per-key limiters give per-tenant bulkheads.
Service meshes enforce bulkheads at the platform layer: an Istio DestinationRule's trafficPolicy.connectionPool caps tcp.maxConnections, http.http1MaxPendingRequests and http.http2MaxRequests per upstream host, enforced by Envoy alongside its circuit-breaking limits.
Netflix's concurrency-limits library replaces hand-tuned static partitions with per-dependency adaptive limits (Vegas and Gradient algorithms modelled on TCP congestion control) that shrink the concurrency budget automatically as downstream latency rises, e.g. separating live from batch traffic on one gRPC server.
Envoy maintains per-upstream-cluster connection pools and circuit-breaking limits, while Kubernetes ResourceQuota caps aggregate namespace CPU, memory, or object use; both are platform-level capacity partitions rather than application call-site wrappers.

quantity
units of measure
dimensioned value
Represent a dimensioned measurement as one value that carries its amount together with its unit, so that conversion, comparison, unit-compatible arithmetic and amount-plus-unit input/output all have a single owner and incompatible units cannot be combined by accident.
Measurements are stored as bare numbers whose unit lives only in a variable name, a column comment or the reader's memory: the same physical quantity appears in metres in one place and in feet in another, conversion factors are retyped at every call site, adding two numbers of different dimensions compiles (or runs) happily, and parsing and formatting '3 km' is reinvented per feature. The recurring trigger is that an amount and its unit always change together and are one conceptual whole, so leaving them as two unconnected things makes the unit rules impossible to own.
Value-scope code in domain, engineering or integration layers that handles physical quantities - length, mass, time, temperature, energy, data volume, concentration. It pays off when values arrive with heterogeneous units (sensors, imports, user input, third parties), when derived quantities such as speed or density are computed, when users select a unit system for display, and when values must survive persistence and transport. The language decides how much of the guarantee is compile-time (units as type parameters, phantom/branded types) and how much is a runtime value object backed by a conversion table or unit registry.
Sensor and telemetry pipelines where readings arrive tagged with a unit and must be normalised to a canonical unit before aggregation, alerting or storage.
Engineering and simulation code (CAD, robotics, structural, electrical) that computes derived quantities such as velocity, torque or energy and must keep the dimensions consistent.
Logistics and commerce where weight, dimensions and rate limits are expressed in different unit systems (kg/lb, cm/in, m^3/ft^3) and are displayed in the customer's chosen system.
Healthcare and laboratory systems that exchange doses and results between systems (mg/kg, mmol/L) with reference ranges in different units.
Energy and utility metering, where consumption (kWh, m^3) is billed through unit-price arithmetic and readings must be comparable across meter types.
UI-level unit-system switching: store and compute in one canonical unit, render and edit in metric or imperial according to a user preference.
Scientific Python applications built on Pint's UnitRegistry, such as sensor and laboratory pipelines, where quantities are parsed, converted and reduced dimensionally at integration boundaries.
.NET engineering and telemetry services using UnitsNet's strongly typed Length, Mass and related quantities, with parsing, conversion, serialization and display-unit selection centralized in the library.
Compile-time dimensional-analysis code using F# units of measure or C++ Boost.Units for simulation and control loops, where invalid unit arithmetic is rejected before runtime and derived units are expressed algebraically.

page-controller
model-1
Give each logical page or form its own input controller that handles the requests addressed to it — reading the request, invoking domain logic and choosing the view — instead of routing every request through one shared handler.
Dynamic pages repeat the same request handling: parse and validate the incoming request, call domain logic, pick a view, report errors. Without a per-page home for that logic it either spreads into templates or gets copied into every script; the recurring decision is whether one page or form owns its request handling, or whether a central controller multiplexes all of them.
Server-side web presentation where URLs map one-to-one onto logical pages, forms or actions: CGI programs, servlets and JSP pages, controller actions, Razor Pages, route handlers in micro-frameworks. It fits sites whose pages share little behaviour, page-focused areas of larger applications, and frameworks whose native unit is a page; it stops fitting as soon as most pages need the same authentication, internationalisation, layout or tracing.
Small to medium websites where each page has its own URL, its own data and its own template (CMS front ends, marketing pages with forms, internal tools).
Form-heavy areas where one page owns one interaction end to end: show the form, validate the submission, run one workflow, render the result.
Prototypes and scripting-era deployments where one program, servlet or route function per page is the natural deployment unit.
Page-focused corners of a larger application (account settings, an admin console) whose pages genuinely differ from one another.
Frameworks whose canonical unit is the page itself: Razor Pages (PageModel = Page Controller), ASP.NET Web Forms code-behind, Java Struts Actions, Django FBV (Function-Based Views) mapped one-per-URL, Flask route functions, PHP single-file-per-page.
Per-page Ajax callbacks that are tightly coupled to a specific page's data and logic, where extracting them into a shared controller would create artificial coupling.
Situations where page-specific code is large enough to warrant a dedicated class but small enough that a full command-object framework is overkill.
ASP.NET Core Razor Pages: each PageModel owns the handlers and view data for one page, with OnGet/OnPost methods providing a concrete page-controller unit for page-specific forms. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/razor-pages/?view=aspnetcore-10.0
Django function-based views: URLconf maps a URL pattern to one Python view function that receives HttpRequest and returns the page response, making small page-specific interactions explicit. https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/6.1/topics/http/views/
Flask route functions: the route decorator binds a URL and HTTP methods to one view function, a lightweight Page Controller shape for independent pages and forms. https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/quickstart/

higher-order-component
HOC
component enhancer
Add cross-cutting behaviour to many components at once by wrapping them in an enhancer function that takes a component and returns a new, enhanced component, so no wrapped component knows about the concern or has to be edited.
The same cross-cutting logic - subscribing to a data source, checking a permission, firing analytics, injecting a theme, a translation or a feature flag - is needed by many components, and copying it into each one couples every component to the concern, re-couples them to every change of it, and leaves the behaviour to be remembered at each new call site. React tried mixins and inheritance first and removed them (implicit dependencies between mixin and component, name clashes, snowballing coupling), so the recurring decision is how to apply one behaviour to many components without editing them, while the components stay reusable and unaware of the enhancement.
Component-model UI code where components are values the framework mounts with a stable identity (React and its ecosystem first; the same shape recurs with Compose composables, SwiftUI views, Blazor components, Scala.js layers and handler-based Go/Java web UIs), where the concern is genuinely cross-cutting rather than local to one screen, where the enhancement can be expressed as a pure function from component to component and applied once at the definition or export site, and where the wrapped component's inputs form a prop-like contract that can be extended by injection without touching its internals.
Subscribing many components to an external data source — React documentation's withSubscription example, or Redux's connect: store state arrives as injected props with no component knowing about the store.
Apollo Client data injection: graphql(Query, { options, props }) HOC maps query results and loading state to props; multiple graphql HOCs composed with @compose; historically the standard before useQuery.
Authorization and feature gating at the boundary: withAuthorization(Component, { requiredRole }) or withFeatureFlag(...) decides rendering without editing the component; useful for route-level guards applied across many pages.
Analytics, telemetry and instrumentation applied at export sites (withAnalytics): tracking calls stay out of presentation code and can be added or removed at one location per module.
Injecting ambient context into components that take it as props — translations via withTranslation (react-i18next), routing via withRouter (React Router v5 and below), theming via withTheme (Material-UI v4) — enabling third-party and vendored components to participate without modification.
Error and loading boundaries as an enhancer (withErrorBoundary): the boundary exists as a component in the tree anyway; an enhancer consolidates the concern into one reusable definition rather than repeating the try/catch at each call site.
Sharing logic into class components and older codebases where hooks cannot be used: the HOC reaches class components and library component-shaped APIs that hooks cannot wrap.
Material-UI v4 theming: withStyles and withTheme HOCs inject classes and theme as props; compose chains combine styling with data (connect + withStyles + graphql on the same export).
Internationalization testing: export both wrapped and unwrapped components; tests use the raw component with a mock t function while integration tests use the full I18nextProvider setup.
Conditional prop injection: a data-enhancer that only injects props when a condition is met (e.g. user is authenticated) lets the wrapped component remain agnostic about the absence of that data.
React Compiler (React Forget) compatibility: heavy HOC layering reduces the compiler's static analysis surface and may cause it to bailout — test compiler output when adding HOCs to a compiled codebase; prefer hooks for new logic the compiler should see.
React Server Components boundary: a HOC that calls hooks or reads client-only context (useAuth, useTheme, useRouter) cannot execute during a server render; the wrapped component may receive undefined injected props on the server and flash-change on hydration. Pass server-fetched data as props through the HOC boundary from a server parent instead.
Streaming SSR and Suspense integration: a HOC that wraps a component behind a Suspense boundary adds a node that may delay streaming; if the HOC itself is async it must be carefully placed to avoid blocking the fallback from showing.
Partial hydration patterns: on islands architectures (Next.js App Router, Astro), a HOC that subscribes to client-side state forces the entire island to be hydrated even if the wrapped component has no server payload; prefer passing hydrated state as props from a server parent.
Recompose (acdlite): a 'lodash for React' utility belt built entirely from composable HOCs (withState, mapProps, pure, branch) piped through enhance/compose - the pattern industrialised; its October 2018 deprecation in favour of Hooks (bug-fix maintenance only) is the canonical case study of the pattern's cost when a runtime offers a cheaper reuse primitive.
MobX React binding: observer from mobx-react / mobx-react-lite is an official HOC that subscribes the wrapped component to every observable read during render, re-rendering it automatically; MobX guidance is to apply observer first (innermost) when composing it with other HOCs, and to wrap every component that reads observables.

row-data-gateway
row data gateway
row gateway
Give each database row its own in-memory object that mirrors the row's columns and carries the row's own find, insert, update and delete operations, so all data-access code for a table lives in one place instead of being duplicated across the scripts that use it.
SQL text, parameter binding and result-set mapping are re-derived inside every transaction script that touches a table, while the in-memory objects those scripts work with know nothing about the database. No single place knows how one row is read, written and deleted, so a schema change ripples through every script and every new query is another chance to get parameterisation and type conversion wrong.
Applies when business logic is organised as transaction scripts or thin services over a relational schema whose columns map closely to the fields actually used: the gateway mirrors the table structure, no object/relational impedance mismatch is being managed, and identity maps, units of work and lazy loading are either unnecessary or added deliberately as separate patterns. It also fits generated persistence layers, where the gateway classes are produced from schema metadata during the build.
Transaction-script applications (order entry, billing runs, batch imports) where several scripts need the same handful of row-level reads and writes.
CRUD-heavy back-office and admin tooling where a screen edits one row at a time and columns map one-to-one onto form fields.
Legacy or externally owned schemas that must be mirrored rather than reshaped: one gateway per table gives an explicit, reviewable seam between the application and someone else's database.
Generated persistence layers: gateways produced from schema metadata on every build, so the tedious class-per-table work is automated and stays in sync with the schema.
Simple mappings inside an otherwise rich domain model, where a domain object keeps a gateway as its data holder instead of copying field values around.
Reporting and fixture utilities that need reusable, parameterised finders for one table without pulling in a full object/relational mapper.
Laminas\Db\RowGateway and RowGatewayFeature (the official laminas-db implementation) expose one row object with save/delete and can materialize table-query results as row gateways, fitting CRUD screens or transaction scripts that edit individual records.
Zend Framework 1's Zend_Db_Table_Row is a documented legacy row-gateway implementation: table queries return row objects with column access plus save/delete/createRow operations, useful when a simple schema is consumed by row-oriented scripts.
The Go dgw tool generates structs and lightweight Table/Row Data Gateway functions from PostgreSQL metadata, demonstrating the pattern as a code-generation choice when a project wants typed CRUD without a full ORM.

cancellation-token
cancellation signal
cooperative cancellation
Give a caller-owned operation tree a one-way request to stop: pass a read-only cancellation signal through every cancellable call, observe it at safe points, clean up what was acquired, and report a distinct cancelled outcome without pretending that cooperative cancellation is forced termination.
A request handler, background job or UI action starts work that fans out into nested calls, tasks or threads. When the caller disconnects, a deadline expires, the user presses stop or a sibling fails, merely abandoning the result leaves already-started work burning CPU, holding connections and calling dependencies. Force-killing a thread or process can interrupt a critical section and corrupt shared state, while a signal that is not propagated or observed cannot stop the call tree or make its cleanup visible to the joiner.
Use where work can outlive the caller's interest and the runtime exposes checkpoints, suspension points or interruptible waits: request-scoped servers, workers, UI tasks, stream pipelines and batch loops. The operation owns cleanup, cancellation may race any checkpoint, and the design must state what happens when a request arrives after an irreversible side effect or while a dependency ignores the signal.
Request-scoped server work: the handler gets a request signal that fires when the client disconnects or the deadline expires, cancelling in-flight database, queue and upstream calls instead of pinning worker threads and connections after the caller is gone.
UI and mobile tasks: navigating away, closing a window or pressing stop cancels the task tree that loads, renders or downloads for that view, and only that view's tokens are affected.
Graceful shutdown: a supervisor stops accepting work and cancels the token shared by worker loops; every worker stops at its next safe point, flushes and releases resources, and the process exits inside the shutdown budget.
Fan-out with short-circuit: as soon as one subtask fails, or as soon as any one result suffices (hedged or racing replicas), the scope cancels the siblings instead of waiting for all of them.
Batch and stream pipelines: a processor subscribes to the pipeline signal and stops consuming and producing when the pipeline is torn down, abandoning the current chunk when the job's deadline elapses.
Testing and tooling: inject an already-cancelled signal, or one cancelled after N iterations, to exercise the stop path without racing an actual shutdown.
HTTP client redirect and retry cancellation: when a request is redirected or a lower-level retry budget is exhausted, cancel the in-flight operation so the client can proceed with the next action without waiting for a result that is no longer relevant.
Health-check abortion: a liveness probe times out or a readiness check fails mid-flight; cancel the in-progress health metric collection so the pod can be restarted or pulled from service without waiting for a hung check.
GRPC deadline and cancellation propagation: a server receives a client deadline and cancellation token; both must be threaded through every async operation so that an expired deadline or a client disconnect promptly frees server resources.
LLM request fan-out: multiple model providers are queried in parallel; the first successful response wins and all pending requests are cancelled immediately, avoiding wasted compute on a result that will be discarded.
Database connection pool eviction: a query timeout or client disconnect cancels the in-flight query, releasing the connection back to the pool before the server's statement timeout fires; the pool's token is derived from the request context so pool eviction and request cancellation share the same stop signal.
Container orchestrator graceful shutdown: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM and waits the terminationGracePeriodSeconds; the application maps SIGTERM to a cancellation token that is shared by all in-flight request handlers, background workers and health-check loops, giving each the termination budget to drain cleanly.
Interactive search with typeahead: each keystroke cancels the previous search task and starts a new one; the token for the previous task is cancelled immediately on the next keystroke, preventing stale results from overwriting fresher ones.
File transfer with resume support: a large upload or download uses chunked transfers; cancelling the transfer sets a flag that causes the next resume attempt to verify which chunks were already received before retransmitting from scratch.
Event streaming with backpressure: a consumer reading from a message queue or Kafka partition uses the cancellation token to stop reading when the application is shutting down or the consumer group is rebalanced, committing its offset before exiting.
Machine learning inference pipeline: a batch inference job can be cancelled when a new model version is deployed or the job's priority drops; the cancellation token is checked between batches so that partial results are preserved and the job can resume without reprocessing completed chunks.
ASP.NET Core's HttpContext.RequestAborted token is passed into HttpClient, database and other long-running operations so a client disconnect or server abort releases work that can no longer contribute to the response.
Go net/http handlers propagate Request.Context through database/sql QueryContext and RPC calls; cancelling the request context closes the subtree's Done channel so backend goroutines can stop and return their resources.
Kotlin kotlinx.coroutines Job cancellation follows structured parent-child scopes, so a screen, request or worker scope can cancel its child coroutines while finally blocks release resources and CancellationException remains distinguishable from failure.
Node.js and browser fetch cancellation: AbortController.signal is passed as { signal } to fetch, EventTarget listeners and streams, so abort() tears down the socket and pending promises; AbortSignal.timeout and AbortSignal.any combine a deadline or several triggers into one signal without polling.
Database query abortion over a side channel: PostgreSQL's frontend/backend protocol sends a CancelRequest on a separate connection carrying the backend PID and secret key, letting a client that gave up - or an administrator via pg_cancel_backend - abort a running query without killing the session.
TPL/PLINQ cancellation acknowledgement: a delegate that throws OperationCanceledException carrying the supplied CancellationToken is treated by the Task Parallel Library as a cancellation acknowledgement rather than a fault, so joiners observe a cancelled task instead of an aggregated error.

question: Choose how each expected payment rejection is represented and propagated so its category and field survive the full parsing, validation, and reservation flow.
answers:
either
Either monad
disjoint union
Encode the two outcomes of a fallible operation - a value-carrying success (Right/Ok) and a reason-carrying failure (Left/Err) - in one sum-type value, so a caller must destructure both branches before going further and failures cannot escape as exceptions, sentinel values or undocumented convention.
An operation can fail in ways the caller must handle, but the failure channel is invisible in the signature: exceptions unwind past intermediate callers, where they get swallowed or merely logged, status codes and sentinels are silently ignored, and the reason for failure is flattened into a message string nobody can branch on.
Expected, recoverable failures in code that has to compose: parsing and validation at a boundary, persistence and I/O calls, service calls inside a pipeline, or any layer whose caller must render, translate, retry or count the failure. It pays off where the error type is part of an API contract between teams or modules, and where the language can express a two-case type (algebraic data type, sealed hierarchy, discriminated union) or a library supplies one.
Validating untrusted input at a boundary and returning the concrete reason (field, offset, rule violated) so the caller can render a precise message.
Domain operations that can fail for several business reasons (insufficient funds, account closed, limit exceeded) where callers must branch on the reason instead of guessing from a string.
Parsing and decoding (config, documents, wire formats) where the failure position or cause must travel back with the outcome.
Pipelines of fallible steps (authenticate -> load -> transform -> persist) that should stop at the first failure with the original reason intact instead of unwinding with a stack trace.
Translate-once boundaries: turn transport errors into domain errors in one adapter, so no layer above has to know about HTTP codes, IOExceptions or database error numbers.
Accumulating validation of independent fields, where every reason must be reported together rather than only the first one — use an Applicative validation instance with a Semigroup-based error accumulator.
Callbacks and async APIs whose failure cannot be thrown to the caller (completion handlers, event consumers) and therefore has to be delivered as a value.
Parallel fallible operations where you want to collect all successes and all failures separately before deciding, using partition or sequence operations on a List<Result>.
Domain-driven design aggregates where a root entity operation can fail for many reasons (invariant violations, business rule breaches) and the aggregate root returns Either to the application layer.
Service-to-service calls inside a pipeline where the downstream service returns a structured error response (not an exception), and the upstream must branch, translate, or propagate it.
Rust standard-library convention: fallible I/O, parsing and system calls return Result<T, E> and ? propagates the first Err up the call chain to a boundary (a main or entry point that returns Result) - the backbone of recoverable error handling in Rust.
Kotlin/Arrow typed-error pipelines: an either { } computation DSL where bind() short-circuits on Left and Either.catch turns a throwing interop call into a Left at the adapter boundary.
Java services using Vavr's right-biased Either: map/flatMap chains propagate Left without checked exceptions, keeping the failure type part of the signature in fluent pipelines.

result
result type
railway oriented programming
Make every fallible step return one value that carries either the success payload or the failure reason, so failures travel with the data along a short-circuiting error track instead of unwinding around it as exceptions, sentinels or out-of-band status codes.
Expected, recoverable failures have no place in the signature: an exception named only in prose unwinds past every intermediate caller and can be swallowed on the way, a status code or sentinel return is silently ignored, and a reason flattened into a message string cannot be branched on. The same mistake then repeats - callers forget the error channel, treat a failure as data, or discover a missed case in production - because nothing in the code forces the failure to be seen.
Code that composes several fallible steps and whose callers must branch on the outcome: parsing and validation at a boundary, application services mapping domain failures to transport responses, I/O and integrations where not-found, conflict and unavailable must be told apart and retried selectively, and pipelines of transformations. It applies wherever the language can express a two-case value (sum type, sealed hierarchy, discriminated union, stdlib Result-like type) and can chain such values (?/and_then/bind/for-comprehension), and it suits runtimes where exceptions are unavailable, expensive or discouraged - C, Go, embedded, WebAssembly, FFI boundaries.
Input validation and parsing chains (parse, then validate, then normalize) where any step may fail and the outermost handler renders the failure; accumulating realizations report every field error at once.
Application and use-case services whose transport layer maps domain failures to status codes, problem documents or process exit codes - the failure must be branchable, not a message string.
Persistence and integration calls that must distinguish not-found, conflict, permission and unavailable and act differently (retry, compensate, return 404).
Retry and fallback policies that need a classification boundary: transient versus permanent is a property of the failure value, not of an exception type tree.
Runtimes without exceptions or where they are undesirable: C libraries, embedded code, WebAssembly, FFI boundaries, and Go services following the (T, error) convention.
Asynchronous pipelines where a rejected promise or future destroys the reason (unwrapped rejection, CompletionException); ResultAsync-style types keep the failure typed across the async boundary.
Batch jobs and migrations that must finish the batch and report which items failed, instead of aborting the whole run on the first exception.
Rust's standard-library std::result::Result<T, E> makes recoverable I/O and parsing failures explicit, and the ? operator propagates Err values without losing their typed cause.
F# Core's Result<'T,'TError> and Result.bind support validation pipelines that return either Ok or Error and pattern-match once at the boundary.
Go's standard-library error values and errors.Is/errors.As provide an explicit, inspectable failure channel for service and integration code without exception-based control flow.

guard-clause
early return
early exit
Reject invalid input, impossible state and failed preconditions at the top of a callable with an immediate exit - return, throw, break or trap - so the remaining body runs only on the happy path and stays flat.
A function that validates as it goes buries its normal path inside nested conditionals: every check adds a level of indentation around the work that follows, the else branch becomes the real body, and a failure discovered halfway down surfaces far from the input that caused it. The recurring decision is where the negative cases go - wrapped around the happy path, or pushed in front of it as prerequisites that exit immediately.
Applies inside function and method bodies in any paradigm: argument checks on public entry points and constructors, request handlers, parsers and deserialisers, worker loops, and C functions that must release resources on failure. The pattern is local to one callable - the decision it settles is how that body is shaped - so it composes with, rather than replaces, signature-level error contracts (Result, Option, Either, exceptions) and with boundary-level validation layers.
Public API, command-handler and constructor entry points: reject null, empty and out-of-range arguments before any state changes, so a failure cannot leave partial work behind.
Deserialisers and parser steps: exit with None/Err at the first unparseable token instead of threading a validity flag through the rest of the parse.
Worker and event loops: a continue guard skips items that fail preconditions without indenting the processing body inside another conditional.
C functions that acquire several resources: argument guards before the first acquisition, then goto-chain exits for the failures that occur while resources are held (CERT MEM12-C).
Server request handling: cheap format and authentication checks at the top of the handler, leaving business logic at the top indentation level (pairs with Intercepting Validator when the same band repeats across handlers).
Test fixtures and doubles: guard the arrange step with explicit assumptions so a test fails loudly instead of exercising a degenerate object.
Cloud event handlers (AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, Cloudflare Workers): guard at the top of the handler before any SDK call or I/O, ensuring no partial state is committed when a precondition fails and the response is short-circuited.
Middleware and edge computing pipelines: each middleware stage acts as a guard that either passes (await next()) or returns a terminal Response immediately (auth rejection, rate-limit exceeded), short-circuiting the chain before downstream handlers run.
Data pipeline transforms: schema-conformance guards check record shape before expensive field-level transformations, failing the entire step fast rather than producing malformed output.
gRPC and service-to-service RPC entry: proto-validated input guards run before any business logic in the handler, rejecting malformed or unauthorised requests with the appropriate status code.
Swift's guard statement (introduced in Swift 2): Apple requires its else branch to transfer control out of the scope, so optional bindings and preconditions stay available to the flat happy path.
Rust's ? operator and let-else: the Rust Reference documents error propagation and diverging pattern guards that return Err or None before later work executes.
ASP.NET Core middleware: a component can short-circuit the request pipeline by omitting next.Invoke or using Run, returning a terminal response before downstream middleware runs.

extensible-visitor
extensible visitor pattern
extensible visitors with defaults
Keep the visitor open on both axes at once - new element kinds and new operations arrive without editing or recompiling any visitor that already exists - by giving every visitor a default method that catches element kinds it was not written for, introducing extended element kinds under an intermediate base whose accept hooks overload (not override) accept, and extending an operation by subclassing the existing concrete visitor so it inherits every case it already handled.
A classic Visitor is cheap in one direction only: a new operation is a new visitor, but a new element kind forces every visitor to grow one more method, so shipped visitors must be edited and redeployed. The trigger is an element hierarchy that is extended by parties who do not own the operations - language dialects, plugin node types, versioned grammars, third-party message formats - where the existing operations must keep working unchanged on the extended structure.
Recursively defined element hierarchies (abstract syntax trees, intermediate representations, document and message models) that grow over time, in a statically typed language whose visitors are concrete classes or interfaces with default bodies, and where the traversal logic itself lives inside the operations. It pays off when old operations must run against new element kinds and when element kinds are added by a different team than the operations; it assumes the visitor protocol can carry a default case and that a runtime type test is acceptable on the dispatch path.
A compiler front-end whose node kinds are extended by language dialects while every existing analysis pass keeps running unchanged (the extensible-compiler case the pattern was derived from).
An IDE or linter analysing a versioned language grammar: the version-1 analysis must not be recompiled when version 2 adds syntax nodes it does not understand.
Plugin systems where third-party modules contribute new node types (document formats, workflow elements, protocol messages) to a host that ships the operations.
Optimisation or lowering pipelines whose passes are shipped separately from the node hierarchy: the platform team adds representations, users add passes.
A published visitor API where other teams implement visitors and the element set grows every release, making 'which kinds does this visitor handle' an explicit, versioned contract.
Migration and validation tooling that must keep working on messages produced by newer producers than the tool itself.
Serialization and schema-generation frameworks such as Jackson's JsonFormatVisitor API, which uses a visitor to traverse Java type hierarchies for JSON/XML schema generation and allows third-party serializers to contribute handlers for new POJO shapes without modifying the core framework.
Query engines over tree-structured data (e.g. Apache Calcite's relational algebra, Rascal's AST analysis): new relational operators or AST node types are contributed by extension modules while existing optimisers and evaluators continue to function unchanged.
Static analysis and bug-finding tools (Coverity, CodeQL, ESLint plugin architectures): new checker plugins add new node-type coverage while the core traversal engine ships unchanged, and old checkers degrade gracefully over unknown node types.
Game engine entity-component systems: new component types are contributed at runtime while existing systems (physics, rendering, AI) continue to process entities; the visitor with default case handles component types added after a given system was written.
Python's ast.NodeVisitor: visit() dispatches to a visit_<Node> method and falls back to generic_visit as the built-in default case, so analysis tools written before newer node kinds existed (Match, TryStar, TypeAlias) keep traversing Python's evolving AST unchanged, exactly the degrade-don't-break contract of the pattern.
The JDK Compiler Tree API (com.sun.source.tree.TreeVisitor / SimpleTreeVisitor): every visit method defaults to visitOther/defaultAction as the catch-all, so javac-based tooling written against Java 8 trees keeps compiling and running as Java adds records, patterns and switch labels - old visitors land in visitOther instead of failing.
Roslyn's CSharpSyntaxVisitor / CSharpSyntaxWalker: the generated visitor carries one Visit method per syntax node kind plus DefaultVisit as the default case, and each C# language version extends the node hierarchy while existing analysers and the compiler's own passes keep working over the extended tree.

active-record
active record pattern
ActiveRecord
Make a domain object the record for one database row: keep the row's state, row-local behavior, and the methods that find and persist it together, so a small domain does not pay for a separate mapping layer.
A simple relational domain still needs a choice about where persistence lives. A Data Mapper or gateway separates table I/O from the object but adds mapping code and a second place to navigate, while direct SQL leaks schema knowledge into callers; the recurring question is whether one row object can own its data and CRUD without hiding transaction boundaries or pretending to model cross-row rules.
A relational store is the single system of record, the domain is small and its rules are mostly local to one row (validation, derivations, simple state transitions), and the team prefers a convention-driven persistence layer over a designed one. Typical homes are framework ecosystems where the ORM is the house style (Rails, Laravel Eloquent, Django, GORM, Vapor Fluent, TypeORM), CRUD-heavy applications, and thin layers over an already well-shaped legacy schema. Entity Framework Core can host behavior on entity classes, but its DbContext and mapping conventions are a Data Mapper-shaped boundary rather than pure Active Record. It stops applying as soon as invariants span several objects, several representations of one table are needed, or the store must be swappable.
CRUD-heavy applications where most screens and endpoints map onto a single table: forms, admin back offices, catalogs, content management.
Small-to-medium domains whose rules are mostly per-row - field validation, derived values, one-row state transitions - so a mapper layer would move data around without adding a model.
Prototypes and thin service layers over an existing, already normalised legacy schema where the table shape is stable and the domain is the schema.
Framework-default persistence: a Rails, Django, GORM, Vapor Fluent or TypeORM codebase where fighting the ORM for purity costs more than it returns.
Simple record-shaped bounded contexts inside a larger system - settings, audit entries, lookup tables - where a full domain model would be overhead.
JSON:API or REST backends for SPAs and mobile apps where the data model maps directly to a relational schema with minimal transformation.
Microservices with a single-responsibility data store: a service whose entire bounded context is one aggregate root table or a handful of tightly coupled tables.
Batch import pipelines where records are validated once and bulk-inserted (insert_all/upsert_all), and the domain logic has already been applied before the bulk operation.
Multi-tenant SaaS backends where row-level isolation is enforced at the database and the ORM connection handles tenant scoping automatically.
Real Rails systems such as GitLab and Discourse are good fits for row-shaped users, posts, permissions and settings backed by PostgreSQL; keep their reporting and cross-record workflows in query or service boundaries.
A Django or Laravel CRUD surface such as an admin or back-office module fits when each request mostly validates, loads, changes and saves one model; switch to a mapper or repository when the same data feeds materially different contracts.

strategy
policy
Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one behind a common operation, and make them interchangeable, so the algorithm a context executes can vary independently of the context and its clients - including at run time.
One class supports several variants of the same computation - sort orders, pricing or tax rules, routing and backoff policies, compression codecs - and the variant has to be selected at run time.
