Multi-granularity lock hierarchies in database systems: coarse area/file locks for large scans paired with fine row locks for point updates, using intention-lock protocols (IS/IX/SIX) to prevent deadlocks.
Kubernetes control plane: kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager contend for a single coordination.k8s.io Lease object — one coarse lock covering a whole controller, renewed at about half the lease duration, with resourceVersion optimistic concurrency so only one candidate can hold it.
CockroachDB epoch-based node leases: one lease per node covers every Raft range that node holds instead of one lease per range, cutting lease-renewal traffic; bumping the node's liveness epoch revokes all of its range leases at once.
JPA/Hibernate applications locking an aggregate with a single LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE on the root row (SELECT … FOR UPDATE) and relying on the root's @Version column as the version token for the whole cluster.

producer-consumer
bounded buffer
consumer-producer
Insert a bounded buffer between producers and consumers of work items so the two sides run concurrently at their own rates, the buffer absorbs bursts and slack, and its bound turns overload into backpressure, queueing or an explicit drop policy instead of unbounded growth.
Production and consumption proceed at different rates: a fast producer outruns its consumer and either drops items or grows a backlog until memory runs out, a slow producer leaves consumers idle, and bursts arrive faster than they can be processed. Wiring the two sides together directly also couples their lifetimes and schedules - a synchronous hand-off makes the faster side wait for the slower - so neither side can be scaled, restarted or tested on its own.
Concurrent in-process software (threads, tasks, coroutines, event-loop callbacks) with one or more producers and one or more consumers that can run at the same time but not at the same average rate. The buffer is a component-level data structure owned by the application - a work queue for a thread pool, a pipeline hand-off, a logging or telemetry sink - not a durable broker, so the decisions are how to hand items over, how to bound the queue and how to end the arrangement cleanly.
Work queues behind thread or worker pools: request handlers enqueue tasks and a fixed set of workers consumes them, so pool size is independent of the arrival rate. Industry examples: Celery (Python), Sidekiq (Ruby), BullMQ (Node.js) all use this shape with Redis or a broker as the durable backing store.
Asynchronous logging and telemetry: hot paths enqueue records cheaply while a background writer drains, formats and writes them, keeping I/O latency off the request path. Structured log collectors (Fluent Bit, Vector) ingest from many sources into one consumer.
Multi-stage data pipelines (decode - transform - encode, extract - transform - load): bounded queues between stages give each stage its own workers and let a slow stage backpressure a fast one. Used in media transcoding, ETL workflows, and stream processors.
Ingestion buffers: a socket, file or broker reader produces records faster than the processing or indexing stage can absorb them, and the buffer smooths the mismatch without dropping data. Common in IoT telemetry ingestion, click-stream collection, and log aggregation.
UI/host integration: a background thread posts work or results to the main/event-loop thread's queue and vice versa, keeping the UI responsive without locks around application state. All major GUI frameworks (Qt, Swing, Flutter) use this internally.
Batch job scheduling: producers enqueue compute jobs (image resize, PDF generation, report creation) and a pool of consumers processes them. Systems like Celery, Hangfire, and AWS SQS follow this pattern, often with priority queues, delayed execution, and dead-letter routing.
Event streaming pre-processing: a Kafka, Pulsar, or NATS consumer-producer chain filters, transforms, and routes events through a series of bounded queues before landing in a data warehouse or search index.
Simulation and testing: a producer generates a deterministic stream of items while a consumer asserts on what it receives, with a sentinel marking the end of the stream. Property-based testing frameworks use this to drive scenario generation.
Print spooling and document processing: print jobs or document conversion tasks are queued and processed by a pool of workers, with bounded queues preventing runaway memory use even under burst load.
ML inference pipelines: a model-serving host receives requests via an API, enqueues them into a bounded queue, and a pool of worker coroutines or threads dequeues and runs inference. The queue decouples HTTP latency from inference latency and provides backpressure when the model GPU is saturated. Tools like Ray Serve, Triton Inference Server, and TorchServe use this shape.
Streaming audio/video processing: a media pipeline (capture - encode - mux - stream) uses bounded queues between stages; frames that arrive during a temporary encoding stall are buffered rather than dropped, and a full encoder output queue backpressures the camera capture stage to prevent unbounded memory growth from frame accumulation.
WebSocket connection management: a server's accept loop enqueues new connections into a bounded connection queue; a pool of handler coroutines or threads dequeues and upgrades them, preventing connection exhaustion under burst load while the handler pool limits concurrency independently of the arrival rate.
Financial order processing: high-frequency trading systems receive market data feeds (producer) and route orders through risk checks and execution engines (consumers), with bounded queues between stages preventing downstream latency from backpressuring the market data ingestion and applying backpressure to upstream feed handlers.
Go channel pipelines: a source goroutine produces values into a channel, transformation stages consume and emit through downstream channels, and a sink drains the final stage. Go's documented pipeline pattern makes channel closure and cancellation part of the producer-consumer lifecycle.
Python asyncio worker queues: an asyncio.Queue(maxsize=N) accepts work from coroutine producers while worker coroutines await get(), process items and call task_done(); finite maxsize suspends producers when consumers fall behind.
Java executor work queues: java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue coordinates multiple producer threads and consumer workers, with put()/take() waiting on full and empty capacity so an Executor-style worker pool can be bounded independently of arrival rate.

pratt-parser
top-down operator precedence
tdop
Parse expressions with many prefix, infix and postfix operators by associating a binding power and a handler with each token type, so precedence and associativity live in one rule table instead of one parsing function per precedence level.
Operator precedence turns expression parsing into a ladder of near-identical functions - one per level - each of which must re-implement associativity, delegate to the next level for its operands, and be edited whenever an operator is added or moves. Grammars with prefix, infix, postfix and mixfix operators (ternary conditionals, assignment, calls, indexing, user-registered operators) make that ladder long, make associativity easy to get subtly wrong, and scatter the grammar across the parser so it cannot be read in one place.
Hand-written parsers for an expression-bearing language, DSL, query or configuration syntax: a token stream is already available (or is cheap to lex), the operator set is large or expected to grow, and the team wants the grammar visible as data. It is typically the expression layer under an ordinary recursive-descent parser for statements and declarations - interpreters, calculators, filter and rule engines, formula tools - and it is unnecessary when a parser generator already declares precedence for the grammar.
Expression evaluators and calculators whose operator set is expected to grow (arithmetic, units, comparisons, percentages, function calls, user-defined functions).
Query, filter and rule languages - search filters, feature-flag conditions, access-policy conditions, spreadsheet formulas - with many comparison, logical and string operators.
Front ends for small languages and DSLs that parse statements and declarations with recursive descent and need real precedence handling for the expression layer.
Single-pass compilers and interpreters that emit bytecode or IR while parsing, where each handler is also the point that emits the operator's instruction.
Template and configuration expression languages that must attach exact source positions and precise errors to every operator.
Host-language extension points that let plugins or users register additional operators at runtime, because registration is just a table entry.
Rust PEG grammars that use pest::pratt_parser::PrattParser to map prefix, postfix and infix operator pairs into calculator or DSL ASTs.
Rust parser-combinator expression grammars built with chumsky's pratt combinator, where atom parsers and prefix, postfix and infix operators declare precedence and associativity.
JavaScript expression-only tooling built on JSEP, where a compact Pratt-style parser produces ASTs and allows custom unary and binary operators with explicit precedence.

assertion
design by contract
Express a model object's preconditions, postconditions and class invariants as executable, side-effect-free predicates at the operations that must uphold them, so a broken contract fails at its boundary instead of remaining a comment or surfacing later as corrupt state. This pattern is for design-by-contract correctness checks, not routine validation of untrusted input or test-only assertions.
Model rules - a balance never below its floor, a period whose end follows its start, a status that cannot move backwards - are left in comments, documents and team memory while constructors and mutators check nothing. A caller can violate a precondition or an operation can break an invariant, allowing invalid state to propagate until an unrelated reader fails; if the assertion is elided by the build, the shipped program may enforce a different contract from the one tested.
Objects with genuine invariants - entities, value objects and aggregate roots - whose state changes through several operations or paths, in a language with an assertion facility, contract syntax or an exception mechanism. The invariant must be expressible as a deterministic, side-effect-free predicate over observable state. Use assertions for programmer/model defects; use always-on validation or typed errors for expected input failures, and decide explicitly whether a release build may elide the check.
Entities and value objects with cross-field rules: an amount that always carries its currency and scale, a date range whose end follows its start, an order whose total equals the sum of its lines.
Aggregate roots that enforce consistency across a cluster of objects: the root asserts its invariant before accepting a change and after applying it.
Domain services and application services checking the preconditions of a use-case operation, so a mis-wired caller fails on the spot instead of writing corrupt state.
Library and framework code that must state its contract: precondition checks on public constructors and methods that clients cannot legitimately violate.
Legacy models under refactoring: assertions turn implicit rules into explicit ones, and where the language strips assertions the same predicates are pasted into the test suite (Evans's fallback).
Reconstitution code that rebuilds objects from stored data, asserting that persisted state still satisfies the model's invariants before the object is used.
Event-sourced aggregates: each state-transition command asserts the preconditions before applying the event, and the event handler asserts the invariant after the state is reconstituted from the event stream.
CQRS write models: the command handler asserts that the incoming command is valid for the current aggregate state before persisting, catching mis-wired or concurrent commands at the write edge.
Microservice boundary contracts: the inbound adapter asserts the precondition of the domain operation before dispatching, preventing malformed commands from entering the domain core regardless of which transport delivered them (HTTP, queue, gRPC).
Money and quantity types: value objects that wrap a numeric amount and a currency/unit, asserting that amounts are non-negative and operations preserve currency matching, preventing silent unit-mixing bugs.
Workflow or saga state machines: assertions on transition preconditions (this status can only advance to that one) prevent illegal state progression from corrupted or out-of-order events.
Property-based test oracle: postconditions double as generative test properties - for all inputs satisfying preconditions, the postcondition holds - turning the same predicate into a specification that a property-based testing library (e.g. Eris for PHP, Hypothesis for Python, fast-check for TypeScript) can falsify.
EiffelBase container classes such as LINKED_LIST and HASH_TABLE: EiffelStudio contract monitoring checks exported-routine preconditions/postconditions and class invariants while the containers preserve their representation rules.
AutoProof-verified Eiffel classes: executable assertions also serve as formal specifications that the verifier can discharge or flag, pairing runtime diagnostics with static proof where available.

range
interval
Represent a span of values as a single interval value whose bound inclusivity and open ends are explicit, so containment and interval-to-interval comparisons live in one place instead of repeated ad-hoc endpoint tests.
Start and end travel together through the code but every caller re-derives what they mean: containment is written as scattered <= / < comparisons that drift apart, "unbounded" is smuggled in as a sentinel value (Long.MAX_VALUE, 9999-12-31), and interval-to-interval questions - do these two overlap, does one enclose the other, what is the gap between them - have no home at all.
Applies wherever a domain concept is a span rather than a point: validity and effectivity periods, booking and availability windows, quantity or price tiers, measurement buckets, version and address ranges, pagination windows, and query parameters such as a date range. It pays off when the same interval is compared repeatedly or crosses a boundary (persistence, API payloads, UI widgets), because the bound convention then has to be written once instead of re-decided per call site. For a single comparison between two local variables the type is pure overhead.
Validity and effectivity windows: a contract, price or membership is valid over [effectiveFrom, effectiveTo), and every check is a membership test against one interval.
Booking and availability: a room, seat or resource is reserved during an interval; overlap (not adjacency) decides whether a new booking is possible, and back-to-back bookings must be allowed deliberately.
Quantity and price tiers: the unit price depends on the quantity interval ([1,10), [10,50), [50, +inf)), so a container of intervals with containment lookup replaces a cascade of if-statements.
Temporal queries and reporting: "last 7 days", "this quarter", "since the migration" are half-open or open-ended intervals passed to repositories and rendered by date-range pickers.
Version, port and address ranges: a compatibility claim covers [1.2, 2.0) of a library, a firewall rule covers a port interval - containment answers "is this covered?" and intersection answers "do these rules conflict?".
Pagination and slicing windows: a page is an interval over a sequence, and half-open semantics make adjacency exact ([0,20) followed by [20,40)),
PostgreSQL range and multirange columns: PostgreSQL's daterange, tsrange and numeric range types make lower-inclusive/upper-exclusive bounds, overlap and containment operators, and indexed range queries part of the persistence contract; choose the bound convention before mapping domain intervals.
Guava Range: Java's Guava Range models convex bounded or unbounded intervals with nine open/closed forms, isConnected and intersection; use ContiguousSet only when a discrete domain really requires enumeration rather than treating the interval itself as a sequence.
Standard-library and container choices: Rust's std::ops::RangeBounds covers included, excluded and unbounded bounds when its range forms fit; for many intervals requiring join/split policies, Boost ICL's interval_set and interval_map supply the container semantics instead of overloading one Range value.

dynamic-router
dynamic routing
rules-based routing
Route each message to a destination chosen from a rule base that can be changed while the system runs, so the router never depends on - or is redeployed for - the set of destinations it serves.
Routing logic hard-coded into the router (switch chains, static filter tables, deployment-time route configuration) couples it to every destination: adding, moving, throttling or retiring a destination needs a code change, a review and a restart, and each topology change forces the router back through the release process instead of being an operational edit.
Message-based integration where the destination set or the routing policy changes faster than the router's release cycle: rules are owned by operations, destinations announce themselves, scale out, or go down for maintenance, or one router instance serves several tenants or environments. Applies when the route can be expressed as rules over message content, headers or context evaluated per message, and the platform offers a usable control channel (config watch, control bus, admin endpoint, hot-reloadable table) to publish rule changes.
Multi-tenant integration hub: each tenant has its own routing table, loaded and swapped per tenant instead of one deployed router per tenant.
Event distribution where downstream teams add or retire consumers by publishing routing conditions rather than requesting a router release.
Canary and blue/green rollouts: send a slice of traffic to a new destination by editing a rule, and roll back by restoring the previous rule set.
Maintenance windows: reroute a destination's traffic to a standby, drain the destination, then restore the rule when it returns.
Regional or sharded routing where the region-to-destination mapping is maintained by operations and changes with capacity, not with code.
Rule-driven enterprise integration in the classic EIP sense, where a rule base is consulted per message and recipients announce themselves on a control channel.
Kubernetes Gateway API traffic splitting: use HTTPRoute weighted backends to shift a configurable percentage of traffic between versions without redeploying the router.
Service mesh canary deployments: an Istio VirtualService or Linkerd ServiceProfile acts as the rule base; routing rules are edited at runtime to steer canary traffic, then promoted or rolled back.
Multi-tenant SaaS routing: Spring Cloud Gateway or Envoy.DynamicRouter loads per-tenant routing rules from a registry, injecting tenant-specific headers or rewrites so one router instance serves hundreds of isolated tenants.
API version routing and A/B testing: route by Accept header, API version path prefix, or experimentCohort header to different backend versions, controlled by rules updated without a release.
Database or cache sharding: route a tenant or user ID hash to the correct shard's endpoint via a rule table that is repointed during resharding without touching application code.
BGP route-server testing: use a chaos-testing framework against a route server to validate that policy changes converge correctly and do not produce route leaks before production deployment.
Traefik dynamic configuration: Traefik builds its routing table at runtime from providers (Docker labels, Kubernetes IngressRoute, Consul/etcd KV stores), so services announce their own routes and rule changes hot-swap without restarting the proxy.
HAProxy Runtime API: add server and set server state/weight over the runtime socket repoint and drain backends without a reload; the Data Plane API layers persistence and validation on top of these runtime changes.
Kong Gateway admin API: Routes - including the expressions DSL when router_flavor is set to expressions - are created and updated at runtime via POST /routes and take effect on the next matching request, with priority-ordered rule evaluation replacing a redeployed config.

request-reply
request-response
request-response messaging
Let a sender obtain a result or a domain error from an asynchronous or remote receiver by pairing each request with a correlated reply, and give the missing reply a defined outcome: timeout, cancellation and disposal of late replies.
Messaging is one-way, but the sender frequently needs a return value or a domain error from the receiver before it can continue. Without an agreed reply destination, a way to match replies to requests, and a rule for what happens when no reply arrives, the caller either blocks forever, mis-associates the next reply with the wrong request, or accumulates pending state it never cleans up.
Asynchronous interaction across a process, thread or network boundary where the caller cannot continue without the receiver's result: HTTP/gRPC-style RPC, broker-based RPC over a queue, actor or thread mailboxes, and browser-to-server exchanges over a socket. It applies when the interaction is naturally one request and one reply, and each exchange has a bounded deadline.
Service-to-service RPC where the caller needs the result to continue (HTTP, gRPC, or a broker-based RPC queue such as the RabbitMQ tutorial's rpc_queue).
Command dispatch that must return a domain error - a validation failure or business rejection - rather than only an acknowledgement of receipt.
In-process actor or thread mailboxes: ask a worker for state with a deadline so the caller can never block forever.
Front-end over a WebSocket asking the server for a value correlated by message id or acknowledgement callback.
Talking to devices, sensors or legacy systems over a socket whose protocol is inherently one request and one response.
Querying a cache or index cluster from a client library where each call is a key lookup with a per-call deadline.
NATS request-reply service calls: a client publishes with a unique inbox as the reply subject and waits for a response under a per-request timeout.
RabbitMQ RPC over an rpc_queue: the client sends reply_to and a unique correlation_id, then matches the worker's response on its callback queue.
gRPC unary RPC: a generated client stub sends one request and receives one response under a propagated deadline, with cancellation available for abandoned work.

double-checked-locking
double-checked locking optimization
DCL
DCLP
Initialise a shared resource exactly once and lazily while keeping the steady-state read path free of lock acquisition - by testing a cheaply published state first and taking the lock only for the one-time construction, where the platform can publish the built object safely to every reader.
An expensive object - configuration, a connection pool, a compiled plan, a cache - must be created once and only when it is first needed, but its accessor is called from many threads. The naive check-then-act form lets two threads build it at the same time, and guarding every read with a lock serialises a path that almost never needs synchronisation. The tempting fix - test a flag cheaply, lock only for the initialisation, test again inside the lock - is sound only if the write that publishes the object is ordered with respect to the readers' loads, which is exactly the part the classic formulation leaves implicit and the reason the idiom is famous for rare, unreproducible failures.
Concurrent, shared-memory software in which one object or cell must be built once and read many times: process-wide singletons and registries, per-object caches inside an object shared between threads, lazily built statics in languages whose runtime also provides the once semantics. The pattern presupposes a memory model with a defined publication ordering (volatile, acquire/release, an initialisation lock, or a runtime once primitive) and a read path hot enough that the lock it removes is measurable. On single-threaded runtimes there is nothing to synchronise, and where a single-threaded composition root can initialise eagerly the pattern is unnecessary.
Process-wide singletons whose construction is expensive or configuration-dependent: configuration snapshot, metrics registry, logger, connection pool, feature-flag view.
Per-object caches inside an object shared by several threads - compiled regular expression or query plan, parsed schema, symbol table - where the build is expensive and the read is hot.
Lazily built statics in languages where the runtime owns the once semantics: C++ function-local static, Swift static let or global let, Kotlin by lazy, Scala lazy val, Go sync.Once, Rust OnceLock/LazyLock.
Compensating for the static-initialisation-order problem: an accessor that builds the global on first use instead of relying on cross-translation-unit initialisation order.
Avoiding lock overhead on a read-mostly, write-once hot path (memo tables, symbol caches, thread-safe lazy proxies) where a contended lock would show up in a profile.
Small or freestanding runtimes without a once primitive, where the first caller must build the cell and an eager initialiser is not available.
RWMutex-protected maps in Go where readers check a fast path before the slower write-locked re-check, as a safer alternative to sync.Map for workloads with known access patterns.
Per-connection or per-session lazy fields in object-pooled servers where the pool itself is the shared cell and each borrowed object gets a lazy-computed field.
Cross-language plugin or extension registries where one language's runtime initialises a global handle that other language shards read without repeated synchronisation.
Rate-limiter or circuit-breaker state that must be lazily built from configuration: building eagerly would couple the policy to startup time, but the read path must be lock-free under high throughput.
Lazy compilation or query-plan warming in database connection pools where the pool is shared but individual plans are built on first use by the owning thread.
Spring Framework's DefaultSingletonBeanRegistry.getSingleton: check the singletonObjects map lock-free, take the singletonLock only when the bean is absent, re-check inside - a production evolution of the idiom whose correctness was formally challenged (SPR-13463) and upheld because the concurrent-map read already carries the needed memory barrier.
Chromium's base::LazyInstance / GetOrCreateLazyPointer: an atomic state word with a 'creating' bit, acquire-load fast path and release-store publication - since deprecated in favour of function-local statics with base::NoDestructor, a signal of how far hardened platforms have moved from hand-rolled DCL.
ACE toolkit's ACE_Singleton<TYPE, ACE_LOCK>: the pattern's original industrial home (the 1997 paper was written alongside ACE) - the template still guards instance() with a double-checked ACE_LOCK acquire and recommends ACE_Recursive_Thread_Mutex for multi-threaded access.
Swift runtime: every global/static let is lowered to swift_once (dispatch_once on Darwin), so the double-checked once structure is the default initialisation mechanism for lazily computed immutable globals rather than hand-written code.

remote-facade
coarse-grained facade
Provide a single coarse-grained facade over a web of fine-grained objects so that a remote client can complete a unit of work in one round trip, while the fine-grained objects keep their local-only interfaces and the facade stays free of domain logic.
An object model tuned for in-process use has small objects with small methods and heavy interaction. Across a process boundary every one of those interactions becomes a marshalling, security and routing event, so one user action turns into dozens of remote calls; the decision is whether, and at which seam, to replace that chatty protocol with a few coarse operations.
Applies at any distribution boundary - a network hop, a service-mesh sidecar or merely a second process on the same host - where a fine-grained object model or service layer must be made remotely usable. It matters most when the interaction pattern is chatty (many small reads and writes per use case), when the model must not be exposed to remote clients, and when the transport is expensive relative to the work being done.
Enterprise application whose rich domain model is consumed by a thick client, another service or a batch job: the service layer gets a coarse remote interface instead of exposing entities and value objects.
Microservice boundary where a use case (place an order, update a shipment) must be a single call while the fine-grained aggregates stay internal to the service.
Legacy integration: a coarse adapter facade over an old object model so that new clients never see the legacy structure and the old model can be refactored behind it.
Mobile or high-latency clients, where every avoided round trip directly improves perceived latency and battery cost.
Batch and offline clients that need bulk operations (fetch a set, submit a set) instead of per-item calls.
Security boundary: one authenticated, authorised and audited entry point in front of the model.
Salesforce Composite API and Composite Graph API: a client submits related record operations, reference IDs and explicit all-or-none/graph boundaries in one request instead of making a remote call per sObject.
Microsoft Graph JSON batching: a `$batch` request groups up to 20 Graph operations behind one HTTP boundary while dependencies and per-request failures remain visible to the caller.
gRPC services such as the official RouteGuide example: generated stubs expose typed unary or streaming RPCs as the remote contract while the server's fine-grained implementation stays local.

monitor-object
thread-safe passive object
monitor
Serialise concurrent method invocations on a shared object by giving the object its own lock and condition variables, so that only one method executes inside it at a time and methods that cannot proceed wait cooperatively instead of polling.
Objects shared by several threads expose their state through ordinary methods, and nothing stops concurrent callers from interleaving inside those methods, corrupting the invariants they were written to maintain. The race is then papered over with ad-hoc locking, sleeps and busy-wait loops scattered through client code. The recurring decision is whether the object itself should own the serialisation (and the scheduling) of its methods instead of leaving that discipline to every caller.
Shared-memory concurrency, where the mutable state of an object is reached by more than one thread and its methods must be atomic with respect to one another. It matters most when some methods cannot run to completion until another method changes the state - a queue that is full or empty, a resource that is not yet available, a phase that has not been reached - because then a method must suspend and later resume, which requires releasing the lock while it waits.
Bounded buffers and work queues shared by producer and consumer threads, where producers wait while the queue is full and consumers wait while it is empty - the pattern's canonical example.
Session, connection or entity registries on a server, where lookups, insertion and eviction must be atomic and callers may have to wait for capacity or for an entry to reappear.
Caches with in-flight bookkeeping (single-flight computation), where a thread that requests an already-computed key waits for the first thread's result instead of recomputing it.
Shared configuration, counters or statistics objects read and updated by request threads, where each call must observe a consistent snapshot of the state.
State machines and simulators whose step methods block until another thread advances a transition, for example a test harness waiting for a worker to reach a known state.
In-process resource pools (connection, database or worker pools) where acquisition blocks until an entry is returned or a timeout expires.
Java's java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue is a fixed-capacity monitor-style bounded buffer: put blocks while full and take blocks while empty, making the producer-consumer coordination explicit.
.NET's System.Collections.Concurrent.BlockingCollection<T> supplies bounded Add/Take blocking, cancellation and completion semantics around a producer-consumer collection; use it instead of hand-rolling Monitor.Wait/Pulse.
Python's queue.Queue provides a thread-safe multi-producer/multi-consumer boundary with blocking put/get operations and optional timeouts, a standard monitor-style primitive for worker pools.

pipeline
assembly line
processing pipeline
Decompose a transformation into an ordered sequence of named stages that each consume the previous stage's output and produce the next stage's input, so the workflow reads top to bottom and every step can be tested, instrumented, reordered or replaced on its own.
A multi-step transformation is written as one long function or a tangle of nested calls: the steps are unnamed, their order is implicit in statement order, intermediate values need throwaway names, there is no seam at which a single step can be logged, tested or replaced, and the same sequence is retyped at every call site that needs it.
Processing that naturally decomposes into successive transformations of the same payload - request handling, ETL, compiler passes, message enrichment, image or byte-stream processing - whether the payload is a single value or a stream. It fits in-process, staged execution where one driver owns ordering, error handling and cancellation; distributing the stages across processes, transports and independently deployed filters is the architectural pipe-and-filter pattern instead.
Request handling: deserialise, authenticate, validate, enrich, persist and render a request, with each step named so a failing stage is attributable and testable in isolation.
ETL and data import: extract, clean, transform, validate and load large files as a stream, so no intermediate collection is materialised and memory stays bounded.
Compiler and interpreter passes: source, tokens, AST, resolution, optimisation and code emission, where each pass is an independent stage over the intermediate representation and the pass list is the pipeline.
Message enrichment in an integration flow: unwrap, translate, enrich and route a message, one stage per concern, with per-channel ordering; the cross-process version stays pipe-and-filter.
Image or byte-stream processing: decode, crop or resize, watermark and encode, lazily per frame or chunk, optionally overlapping stages across cores.
Configuration-driven data cleaning: the stage list is assembled from configuration or a plugin registry so different tenants get different ordered steps without changing the stages themselves.
TensorFlow tf.data input pipelines: tf.data.Dataset pipelines that chain map, prefetch, parallel_interleave and shuffle stages to feed a training loop efficiently, with each stage independently configurable and the whole pipeline testable in isolation.
LLM token streaming: HTTP server-sent event streams where an LLM produces tokens at inference speed while clients consume at variable network speed; stream.pipeline() prevents the inference server from buffering unbounded tokens in memory when a slow client disconnects (Node.js stream backpressure case study).
Observability telemetry pipelines: OpenTelemetry Collector chains receivers, processors (memory_limiter, batch, filter, transform, tail_sampling) and exporters for traces, metrics and logs, with connectors (e.g., spanmetrics) bridging signal types and memory_limiter placed first to prevent OOM before filtering.
Typed TypeScript pipeline with schema validation: Zod or io-ts schemas define the stage contract at each boundary, catching schema violations at the exact stage that produced bad data rather than at a distant consumer.
Async generator pipelines in Python: asyncio queues with bounded capacity connect async generator stages, propagating backpressure by pausing producers when the queue is full; the FinStream analytics case study showed 82% memory reduction and 99.7% latency reduction versus unbounded buffering.
Event-streaming pipelines with Kafka and Flink: producers, topic partitions, Flink consumers and checkpointing form a distributed pipeline where backpressure cascades across every boundary; the Kafka max.block.ms and Flink backpressure.sample.interval settings interact under partition saturation and must be tested together under load.
Dynamic pipeline parallelism: construct-and-run pipelines (MapReduce, Spark) fix stage count at construction, while on-the-fly pipelines (Cilk-P Piper algorithm) allow the structure to emerge at runtime, varying per iteration and supporting data-dependent branching; on-the-fly enables pipelines like x264 that cannot be expressed with a fixed static structure.
LLVM compiler pass pipelines: PassBuilder assembles ModulePassManager, CGSCCPassManager, FunctionPassManager and LoopPassManager across the IR hierarchy (Module → CGSCC → Function → Loop), with registered callbacks injecting passes at named extension points (pipeline-start, vectorizer-start, optimizer-last); incorrect PreservedAnalyses declarations invalidate all downstream analyses.
Continuous data pipelines at scale (Google model): periodic pipelines run on cron and suffer from depth growth and resource exhaustion as organic load increases; continuous pipelines (master-slave or event-triggered) replace idle-waiting with always-on processing, eliminating the 'pipeline vs cron' discontinuity at the cost of operational complexity.
ML pipeline orchestration (Airflow, Kubeflow, Prefect, Dagster): each orchestrator applies the pipeline pattern at the workflow level - Airflow's DAG-of-tasks, Kubeflow's per-container-step pipelines with GPU scheduling, Prefect's monoflow/subflow/orchestrator pattern, and Dagster's software-defined assets where asset dependencies imply the pipeline; the pipeline is the scheduler's unit of execution, not an implementation detail.
Apache Beam: PCollections flow through composable PTransforms (ParDo, Combine and GroupByKey) in a pipeline graph, making each transform boundary explicit while the runner handles execution.
Node.js stream.pipeline(): Readable, Transform and Writable stages compose with built-in backpressure, error propagation and AbortSignal cancellation; this is a concrete streaming realization, not a durable workflow engine.

monad
io monad
programmable semicolon
Give a computation's effect (absence, failure, asynchrony, I/O, state) a type of its own with a unit and a bind operation, so that a sequence of steps in which each step depends on the previous value composes into one pipeline while bind propagates the effect automatically.
Sequencing computations where the next step needs the previous step's result and every step may additionally be absent, failing, asynchronous or effectful pushes the effect handling into the business logic: nested null checks, try/catch ladders, callback pyramids. Every call site repeats the same propagation decision (short-circuit? await? log?) and one forgotten check turns a controlled failure into a crash or a wrong value.
Applies wherever a value and the fact that it is absent, pending, failing or impure belong together: chained lookups, validation and error pipelines, asynchronous call chains, state threading, parser and interpreter pipelines, and effect-typed application cores. It matters most when the sequence is long, when the effect policy must be uniform and testable, and when the language already provides monadic types (Optional, Result, Promise, IO) or syntax that desugars to bind (do-notation, for-comprehensions, async/await).
Chained lookups where any link may be missing: user -> address -> city expressed with Maybe/Optional instead of nested null checks.
Validation and error pipelines in which each step can fail with a domain error and the first failure must short-circuit (Either/Result, railway-oriented programming).
Asynchronous workflows whose next call depends on the previous response (Promise/async-await, CompletableFuture.thenCompose, Kotlin suspend functions, Swift Task).
Effect description and interpretation: building an IO/program value that is pure data and running it through different interpreters in tests and production (IO monad, tagless-final).
State-threading computations such as compiler passes, random generators or incremental traversals written as a State monad pipeline.
Parser combinators and nondeterministic search, where each step consumes the previous parse result or explores every value produced by the previous step (parser monad, List monad).
Rust's std::result::Result composes fallible steps with and_then and the ? operator, returning early on Err while keeping the successful value available to the next dependent step.
Java's CompletableFuture.thenCompose chains dependent asynchronous stages: the function returns another CompletionStage and the outer stage adopts its completion or exceptional failure.
Scala for-comprehensions over Option, collections, or other types with map, flatMap, and withFilter desugar dependent bindings into the corresponding combinators, keeping the monadic sequence readable without hiding its operations.

bulkhead
bulkhead isolation
cell-based architecture
Partition finite shared capacity at the failure domain (dependency, tenant, priority class, or cell) into independently bounded pools or permits, with an explicit queue and saturation policy, so one slow, saturated, or failing participant cannot consume capacity reserved for others.
Several dependencies or tenants share thread, connection, worker, or permit pools. When one becomes slow, leaky, or overloaded, its calls hold shared slots and fill shared queues, so unrelated work queues and fails behind it; the design needs a boundary that contains resource exhaustion without pretending to isolate CPU, network, or server-side limits that remain shared.
Any component whose concurrency is a finite resource: a service calling multiple downstream APIs, a multi-tenant workload, a job runner mixing interactive and batch work, or an inference and gateway tier with per-deployment quotas. The failure mode to contain is degradation and overload (slow dependency, connection leak, traffic spike), not only hard failure, and the isolation boundary must be chosen at the failure domain - instance, dependency, tenant or priority class.
A service that calls several downstream APIs through one shared HTTP client: give each downstream its own connection and thread budget so one hanging endpoint cannot block the others.
Multi-tenant SaaS where one tenant's workload must not consume the concurrency available to other tenants (per-tenant pools).
Interactive request traffic sharing a database with batch or report jobs: separate pools per workload class keep the database from serialising everything behind the batch.
An API gateway or backend-for-frontend routing to many backends with per-route concurrency caps, so a slow backend does not consume the proxy's shared capacity.
Job workers that mix latency-critical and background queues: per-queue worker pools prevent a backlog of background jobs from starving urgent work.
Inference and AI serving where each model deployment has its own concurrency quota and a saturated model must not consume the shared request capacity.
Cell-based architectures: each cell (complete, independent service instance) is a bulkhead partition; load grows by adding cells, and a failure is contained to the single cell — used at AWS, Google, and Netflix scale.
Shuffle sharding: Amazon Route 53-style virtual shard assignment where each tenant is assigned to a random shard of two or more cells; with eight cells and two-per-shard there are 28 unique shards, so a problem affects only 1/28th of tenants — far better than regular per-cell partitioning.
AI and inference workloads: per-deployment or per-tenant Azure OpenAI or LLM deployment quotas prevent one saturated model from consuming the shared request capacity across the platform.
Database RU isolation: Azure Cosmos DB request-unit throughput assigned per container acts as a storage-layer bulkhead; one noisy container cannot exhaust the RU budget of others.
Resilience4j's SemaphoreBulkhead and FixedThreadPoolBulkhead give a JVM service per-dependency permits versus a bounded queue and worker pool; choose based on whether caller threads may be occupied.
Netflix Hystrix's per-command thread pools or semaphore isolation reject work and route it to fallback, containing a slow downstream to its command boundary (historical and deprecated).
.NET services use Polly's BulkheadPolicy/AsyncBulkheadPolicy (maxParallelization plus maxQueuingActions, rejecting with BulkheadRejectedException when both are full); Polly v8 replaced it with ConcurrencyLimiter over System.Threading.RateLimiting, whose partitioned per-key limiters give per-tenant bulkheads.
Service meshes enforce bulkheads at the platform layer: an Istio DestinationRule's trafficPolicy.connectionPool caps tcp.maxConnections, http.http1MaxPendingRequests and http.http2MaxRequests per upstream host, enforced by Envoy alongside its circuit-breaking limits.
Netflix's concurrency-limits library replaces hand-tuned static partitions with per-dependency adaptive limits (Vegas and Gradient algorithms modelled on TCP congestion control) that shrink the concurrency budget automatically as downstream latency rises, e.g. separating live from batch traffic on one gRPC server.
Envoy maintains per-upstream-cluster connection pools and circuit-breaking limits, while Kubernetes ResourceQuota caps aggregate namespace CPU, memory, or object use; both are platform-level capacity partitions rather than application call-site wrappers.

table-module
Organise the domain logic of a table or view as one module with a single instance whose operations act on whole sets of rows, so table-shaped rules are written once against tabular record sets instead of being scattered over per-row objects or per-request procedures.
The rules for a table are set-shaped - recalculating a column across all rows, validating an import batch, posting a period, aggregating or exporting a whole table - and the platform already speaks in tables and record sets (result sets, DataTables, grids, reports). A Domain Model would build one object per row and pay for identity, hydration and per-object behaviour the rules never use, while a Transaction Script repeats the same table-shaped logic in every use case that touches the table.
Data-centric enterprise applications with moderate, table-shaped logic: batch jobs, imports and reconciliation, reporting and export modules, and applications whose UI and data tooling is table-based (typed DataSets, data grids, report engines). It assumes that data access is already provided by a Table Data Gateway or equivalent, and that callers - typically a Service Layer - own the transaction boundary around the module's calls.
Periodic batch posting: recompute balances or fees for every row in a period in one set-oriented pass.
Import and reconciliation: validate, normalise and promote a staging table before its rows become live data, reporting row-level errors as a batch.
Reporting and export modules that fetch a record set for a grid, report engine or CSV/Excel export, where tabular output is the goal.
Bulk recalculation after a rule change: apply a corrected formula to all existing rows of a table without loading them into a model.
Small-to-medium applications where each table has a handful of well-defined operations and no rich invariants spanning rows or tables.
Cleansing and reconciliation jobs over an operational table where the database should do the heavy lifting (aggregate, update ... where) and the application only orchestrates.
.NET ADO.NET typed DataSet / typed DataTable modules: the generated table is the record set, business methods operate over all its rows and it binds directly to grids and report controls.
Ruby on Rails set-oriented surface: an ActiveRecord::Relation scoped to one table applies table-wide rules via update_all/delete_all as a single SQL statement without instantiating row models, whose official documentation warns that validations and callbacks are skipped so the statement must carry the rule.
Django set-wide recalculation: QuerySet.update() and bulk_update() write whole filtered sets with direct SQL that bypasses per-row save(), used exactly where per-object persistence would mean one round trip per row.

compound-components
compound component
compound component pattern
Give a family of cooperating components one owner — the parent — that holds the shared state and publishes it implicitly to every child, so consumers compose the family declaratively while the parent alone enforces its invariants and behaviour.
A widget only works when a parent and its children agree on one piece of state (which option is selected, which panel is open, whether a field is invalid), but the call site is the only place that knows the children. Holding the state at the call site means threading the value and its update callbacks into every child (prop drilling), and holding it in the children means the parent cannot enforce the family's invariants — exclusivity, ordering, keyboard behaviour — nor react to a child's change in one place. The recurring decision is where the shared state lives and how children participate in it without the call site wiring them.
Component-tree UI code: design-system and widget libraries (select/option, tabs, menus, field groups) in frameworks that can inject state into descendants without passing it through props — React context or child cloning, Angular content projection plus DI, Vue provide/inject, Compose CompositionLocal and slot scopes, SwiftUI environment and preference keys, Blazor cascading values, WPF attached properties over the logical tree — and in widget toolkits whose group objects (Swing ButtonGroup, JavaFX ToggleGroup, Qt QButtonGroup, tkinter control variables) play the same role. It pays off where the public API must stay small and the children must stay replaceable; it does not apply in languages without a component tree or without an implicit-injection channel.
Custom select, combobox or autocomplete families built from Option children — the canonical example: the parent owns the selection, the highlight and the keyboard interaction while options only declare their value and label.
Tabs, accordions and menus where Tab/TabPanel/MenuItem children register their identity and the parent owns the active item, the ordering and the ARIA wiring.
Form-field families (Field + Label + Input + Error) that share one validation/invalid state and generated ids without the call site passing them around.
Data-group widgets: tables with Column definitions, list widgets with Item children, tree views with Node children, chart legends with Series children.
Design-system libraries that export one namespaced symbol whose parts must be used together — the context in which the pattern is most often documented and most valuable.
Collapsible panel families (Disclosure pattern) where a parent owns the open/closed state and Trigger/Content children read it — also known as the Disclosure pattern in ARIA authoring practices.
Stepper/wizard widgets where a parent owns current-step state and Step/StepIndicator children read it without the consumer threading step indices.
Popover/tooltip families where a trigger button and a content panel share open/close state through the parent without prop drilling.
Radix UI Primitives — Dialog.Root owns the open/close context and Trigger/Portal/Content/Title/Description consume it, while asChild (Slot) merges each part's props, refs and keyboard behaviour into the consumer's own button or link.
Ark UI headless components (built on Zag.js state machines) — Popover.Root/Trigger/Positioner/Content share state through the root, ids props compose aria bindings across two families, and the same compound anatomy works in React, Solid, Vue and Svelte.
Headless UI's Dialog family (Dialog, DialogBackdrop, DialogPanel, DialogTitle, Description) — the root enforces the dismiss contract (open prop, onClose callback, focus trap, aria-labelledby) and every part reads the shared open/closed state, exposed for styling as data-open/data-closed attributes.

table-data-gateway
table gateway
Confine every SQL statement that touches one table or view inside a single gateway object whose methods take and return plain record structures, so that no other code contains SQL for that table and rows cross the boundary as data rather than as domain objects.
Access to one table is spread across the codebase: SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE fragments are copied into every caller, nobody can say which queries a schema change will break, DBAs cannot find the SQL that needs tuning, and each caller has to know the dialect, the placeholders and the column order. The desired boundary is a single object that mediates all access to the whole table while the individual rows remain records (tuples, structs, hashes, DataRows) instead of becoming mapped objects.
Relational persistence where the database is a stable, schema-first integration point and SQL-level control matters (indexes, hints, bulk loads, vendor features), where the team deliberately does not want O/R mapping machinery in the domain layer, and where the domain logic is simple enough that rows may travel as records - CRUD and query services, reporting/read models, ETL writers, local SQLite stores, or a legacy database mediated for several applications. It is also the packaging decision for 'the SQL has to live somewhere well known' before a DAO, repository or query object is justified.
A service or CRUD application over a handful of tables where every screen maps to a few statements per table and an ORM would add more machinery than it removes.
Reporting and read models: read-only gateways over views or wide tables that return records directly to a formatter, export or BI job.
Legacy databases mediated for several applications: one gateway library per database becomes the documented API and the place where vendor quirks are hidden.
Embedded/local storage (SQLite, SQLCipher) in a desktop or mobile app, where one gateway per table keeps SQL out of the UI and can be tested with an in-memory database.
Batch and ETL writers that need explicit control over statement batching, cursors and transaction size - control that generated mappers hide.
Gradual refactoring of SQL scattered through transaction scripts: the first step is to move each table's statements into a gateway, after which a Data Mapper or repository can be introduced deliberately.
Test fixtures and seeders that must write through the same statements as production code rather than through a second, divergent SQL path.
Generated gateways in Go: sqlc compiles a schema plus a file of named queries into one struct per table and one type-safe method per SQL statement, with the caller holding the database handle and opening transactions - the gateway's invariants are then enforced by the generator and compiler rather than by convention.
Local SQLite storage on Android: each Room @Dao is a gateway over one table - the SQL lives in @Query-annotated methods validated at compile time, rows travel as plain entity data classes, and @Transaction or database-level transactions keep atomic multi-DAO boundaries in the caller.
Java teams that want the gateway structure without hand-writing it: jOOQ's code generator emits one DAO class per table or view (findAll, findById, generated fetchByColumn methods) that reads and writes Record/POJO rows and borrows the caller's Configuration, so the per-table SQL surface is regenerated when the schema changes.

identity-map
first-level cache
session cache
Guarantee that within one session every database row is represented by exactly one in-memory object, by keeping a keyed registry of loaded objects that every load consults before hitting the database.
Two code paths in the same session load the same row into two different objects: updates through one are invisible to the other, the last flush silently wins, and every load pays the remote-call cost again. The catalog states the invariant as: the same row must never be two different in-memory objects in one session.
Object-oriented persistence (data mappers, repositories, unit of work) where entities carry a stable database identity (an Identity Field) and several parts of one business transaction or request refer to the same rows. Applies whenever duplicate in-memory instances would break graph consistency or lose updates - typically inside an ORM session or a hand-written persistence context whose lifetime bounds staleness.
ORM sessions in web request handling (JPA EntityManager, EF Core DbContext, SQLAlchemy Session, MikroORM EntityManager) where several services touch the same entities in one request.
Batch import and synchronisation jobs that re-read the same rows repeatedly inside one transaction and must not operate on divergent copies.
Object graph reconstruction in data mappers, where cycles and shared references need one in-memory instance per row.
Desktop and document applications with a context-scoped object space (Core Data contexts) where objects are edited, undone and saved as one unit.
Hand-written persistence layers over plain SQL where two repositories serve the same table and must agree on identity.
CQRS command handlers where the same aggregate is loaded multiple times within one command execution — the identity map prevents duplicate instances from forming across repository calls within the same session.
Event-sourced aggregate reconstruction: replaying events to rebuild aggregate state requires the same aggregate instance to accumulate state across multiple event applications; identity map guarantees a single instance per aggregate ID per reconstruction session.
Microservices saga and choreography: within one service's unit-of-work, multiple steps may load the same entity; identity map ensures all steps operate on the same instance even when the entity is referenced across different event handlers.
DDD bounded-context integration: when one bounded context holds a reference to an entity from another context (by ID), that entity is resolved through the local identity map — multiple resolution paths must all consult the same map to stay consistent.
Testing scenarios where the same entity is accessed via multiple repository paths: identity map guarantees test assertions see the same instance regardless of which repository method returned it, enabling meaningful state verification.
Multi-tenant applications where each tenant request gets its own session/identity-map scope, preventing cross-tenant data leakage by construction — a shared/global map would allow one tenant's rows to shadow another's.
SQLAlchemy Session.get in a unit of work: repeated primary-key loads return the same Python object from the Session identity map, while the Session is deliberately not a cross-session query cache.
EF Core tracked queries and AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution: the DbContext keeps one entity instance per key for tracked results, while no-tracking identity resolution is opt-in for read models.
Hibernate Session persistence contexts: repeated loads of the same entity type and identifier resolve to the one managed instance per Session, so entity graphs and dirty checking share state.

question: Whether to replace the remote classifier with a test-specific responder that returns selected classifications and raises selected failures to drive each policy branch.
answers:
stub
test stub
stub object
Replace a collaborator with a test-specific stand-in that returns canned answers, so the component under test can be driven down paths - success, empty, error, timeout - that the real collaborator cannot be made to produce on demand.
The component under test receives indirect inputs through a collaborator, and the branch that must be exercised is selected by what that collaborator returns. The real collaborator will not produce the needed value on request: it is slow, remote, licensed, non-deterministic, or simply never returns the rare case - the empty result, the declined payment, the timeout - that the test exists for. Without a controllable replacement the test either cannot reach the path at all or has to provoke it through the production system, which is exactly what unit testing was supposed to avoid.
Unit and component tests of a component whose collaborators are already, or can cheaply become, abstractions: the values and exceptions a collaborator returns are inputs to the component under test, and the test asserts what the component does with them rather than how the collaboration happened. Typical where the collaborator is remote or stateful (HTTP client, database, queue, clock, payment gateway) or where the branch under test is an edge case - empty page, declined payment, expired token, feature off. The pattern assumes a substitutable seam: a constructor parameter, an injected interface, a factory, a lookup, or a patchable module.
Exercising a rare branch of the component: an empty result set, a declined payment, a 429 from a gateway, a missing feature flag.
Testing error handling: programme the stub to raise the exception the real service would raise - timeout, connection reset, malformed payload - and assert that the SUT surfaces or recovers from it.
Unit-testing a component against a collaborator that is slow, paid, unavailable in CI or still being implemented; the stub encodes the agreed response while the real adapter is built.
Removing non-determinism from a path the real collaborator decides by clock, randomness or remote state (token expired, cache cold, retry budget exhausted), so one outcome can be asserted exactly.
View and presentation tests: a fixed dataset from the stub, so the assertion is about the rendering or the decision logic and nothing else.
Boundary values on contract edges - zero, maximum, empty string, unicode payloads - that the real system cannot be asked to return on demand.
Mockito (Java): when(warehouse.hasInventory(...)).thenReturn(false) programmes the declined-branch answer and thenThrow(SocketTimeoutException.class) injects the failure, and consecutive-value stubbing (thenReturn(v1, v2)) drives retry-then-succeed paths that the real warehouse would never produce on request.
Python unittest.mock (standard library): Mock(return_value=...) fixes the canned answer while side_effect set to an exception or an iterable raises or sequences answers per call - the library ships Responder and Saboteur behaviour as first-class configuration.
Moq (.NET): mock.Setup(x => x.HasInventory(...)).Returns(false) and .Throws<InvalidOperationException>() are the canned-answer primitives, so a C# test reaches the empty-inventory and fault branches of Order.Fill without touching a database.

configurable-test-double
configurable test stub
configurable mock object
Configure one reusable Test Double per collaborator role during fixture setup - before the test installs it in the system under test - so the values it returns and the calls it expects are stated as configuration data in the test itself instead of being hard-coded into a purpose-built double class per scenario.
Several tests need the same collaborator role (clock, gateway, repository, notifier) to behave differently: some need canned successes, others exceptions, timeouts or specific call arguments. When every variation is its own hard-coded double class, the suite duplicates double code and the configured behaviour is buried inside the double rather than visible in the test, which is Meszaros' Test Code Duplication and Obscure Tests territory.
Unit tests that isolate a system under test by replacing a depended-on component, where the same collaborator role recurs across many tests with slightly different data or failure modes and a substitutable-dependency seam (constructor or parameter injection, factory, registry, subclass hook) exists to install the double. It covers both construction routes - a hand-built reusable double and a toolkit that statically or dynamically generates one - and both configuration styles, a test-only configuration interface or a record/playback configuration mode.
A collaborator role used by many tests with different canned answers - time provider, pricing or tax service, identifier generator, feature-flag client - where only the returned value varies between tests.
Injecting failures on demand: the double is configured per test to raise timeouts, throw exceptions or return error codes so the error-handling paths of the system under test are exercised without a second double class.
Verifying indirect outputs: expected arguments are configured on the same double and the test asserts afterwards that the right message was sent with the right payload.
A suite-wide fixture double for a slow, unavailable or side-effecting dependency, re-configured per test instead of re-implemented per test.
Generated doubles for collaborators with wide interfaces, where hand-writing a double class would be pure boilerplate and would have to be kept in step with the interface.
Cutting a deep chain of real collaborators during refactoring: one configured double stands in for the chain so fixture setup stops constructing and persisting a network of objects.
Contract testing with external services: configure a double to return contract-compliant responses that verify the system under test produces correctly-formatted requests (see Pact, consumer-driven contracts).
Testing async/await code paths: configure the double to return awaitable results or throw exceptions asynchronously, exercising the calling code's async error handling.
Performance boundary testing: configure a double with deliberate delays or throttling to verify timeout and retry logic behaves correctly under degraded conditions.
State machine testing across transitions: configure the double to return specific state-dependent responses as the system under test walks through a sequence of transitions.
Consumer-driven contract verification: use a mock server (e.g., Pact mock) to record expected interactions, generating a contract that the provider can verify independently.
Testing retry and circuit-breaker logic: configure the double to fail a configurable number of times before succeeding, exercising back-off and recovery paths.
Data-driven test scenarios: parameterize the double's configuration with external data (CSV, JSON) to cover many input combinations without duplicating test code.
Java suites configure one Mockito mock per collaborator interface - when(clock.now()).thenReturn(instant) for indirect inputs, verify(gateway).send(msg) for indirect outputs - replacing hand-built double classes.
Python tests install unittest.mock.patch(..., autospec=True) or create_autospec(...) doubles per test, configuring return_value/side_effect and asserting calls via assert_called_with, with signatures checked against the real object.
Go tests run mockgen (uber-go/mock) over the collaborator interface once and configure expectations during setup - mockFoo.EXPECT().Bar(gomock.Eq(99)).Return(101).Times(1) - since Go offers no runtime proxying.

cache-aside
look-aside cache
lazy loading cache
Place the cache beside the authoritative store and make the application own the protocol: look up the cache first, load the entry from the store on a miss and populate it with a TTL, and invalidate the entry right after each write to the store - so repeated reads stay cheap while the store, never the cache, decides what is true.
A source of truth (relational database, downstream service, object store) is expensive or rate-limited for the read volume an application receives, while most reads repeat a small set of keys: without a cache every request pays the source-of-truth cost, and with an unmanaged cache the copies silently drift. The recurring decision is where the read path looks first, when a miss may populate the entry, and what a write must do so the cached copy stops lying.
Read-heavy paths in front of a slower or metered authoritative store, typically several application instances sharing a Redis or Memcached tier, or each holding an in-process cache, where a bounded amount of staleness is acceptable and every writer can be held to the same invalidation discipline. It applies when the read/write ratio is high, when the cache itself does not provide read-through or write-through, and when lost or evicted entries can always be recomputed from the store.
Read-heavy lookups by natural key (product catalogs, user profiles, article pages) in front of a relational database.
Several service instances sharing a Redis or Memcached tier where every instance must see the same cached copy and the same invalidation.
Reference data that changes slowly (currency rates, feature flags, configuration, price lists) refreshed by TTL with explicit invalidation when it is edited.
Expensive aggregate or derived results (dashboards, search pages, recommendations) recomputed into the cache per request key.
Per-instance in-process caches for hot, rarely changing values where a shared cache would add network latency without adding much.
Multi-level caching in Kubernetes: an in-process L1 (Caffeine) sidecar on each pod with an L2 Redis cluster, where the L1 is invalidated on each incoming request via a bloom filter or pub/sub.
CDN edge caching for static or semi-static API responses: the application server acts as the origin and issues cache-aside reads; CDN edges serve from their own look-aside cache with short TTLs and PURGE invalidation on writes.
RAG and vector cache in AI pipelines: embedding results cached by query hash so repeated semantically identical questions hit the vector store once and reuse cached results; TTL bounds staleness of the embedding index.
Django's low-level cache API (cache.get / cache.get_or_set with a per-key timeout, cache.delete on save) is cache-aside as a framework primitive; MediaWiki's WANObjectCache does the same at Wikipedia scale via getWithSet, invalidating page parses through cross-datacenter purges rather than direct writes.
Spring's cache abstraction applies the pattern declaratively: @Cacheable loads and populates on a miss, @CacheEvict removes the entry after the writer, with RedisCacheManager supplying the TTL - the application still owns both paths, the annotation only moves where.
Hibernate's second-level cache read-write concurrency strategy is a managed cache-aside: the updated entry is soft-locked around the transaction so concurrent readers miss to the database instead of repopulating the cache with the pre-commit value.

durable-subscriber
durable subscription
durable consumer
Keep a publish-subscribe consumer's place while it is offline: the broker binds a stable subscription identity to retained messages or a committed position, then resumes delivery after reconnect until retention, expiry, or quota says the backlog is no longer available.
A subscriber on a publish-subscribe channel can be unavailable during redeployment, maintenance, device disconnects, or scheduled batch work. A non-durable subscription drops messages published during that gap, so the design must choose a stable identity and broker-side state, then make finite retention, replay pressure, and at-least-once redelivery explicit; durable state prevents a gap only while that state remains available.
Broker-mediated publish-subscribe messaging where consumers are intermittently offline but individual messages matter: JMS topics, MQTT sessions, Kafka consumer groups, NATS JetStream durable consumers, cloud topic subscriptions. It presumes the messaging system can store messages (or positions) durably, so it is as much a broker-configuration decision as a client one, and it presumes at-least-once delivery is acceptable once the consumer is idempotent. It does not apply to in-process notification or to broadcast where only the newest value counts.
A Kafka-backed order-processing service that is redeployed or scaled to zero while events keep arriving: the consumer group resumes from its committed offsets and replays what it missed.
An IoT or mobile client on an intermittent link: an MQTT persistent session holds QoS 1/2 publications for its client id and delivers them when the client reconnects.
A partner integration that receives published documents while the partner's system is down: an unshared JMS durable subscription, or a cloud topic subscription, is registered on their behalf and holds the backlog until they acknowledge it.
A nightly audit or analytics consumer that must see every published change: the day's backlog is drained in bounded batches and acknowledged as it is persisted.
A ledger or compliance consumer that must never silently skip events: retention and lag alarms are configured so an offline subscriber is noticed before its backlog expires.
A cloud event-driven architecture (SNS FIFO → SQS FIFO): SNS preserves ordering and deduplication while SQS queues hold messages for durable fan-out to Lambda or EC2 consumers, with DLQs capturing failed deliveries for replay.
An industrial SCADA/IoT sensor fleet where devices connect sporadically over unstable networks: MQTT persistent sessions with a long session expiry interval preserve every telemetry reading until each device reconnects, even after multi-day outages.
A financial audit trail that must immutably record every state-changing event: events are durably retained in Kafka or JetStream and consumed by a compliance subscriber that must not skip or duplicate entries; idempotent deduplication and offset commits after durable persistence enforce this.
A supply-chain or logistics event-sourcing system where downstream services reconstruct state by replaying events after a crash or deliberate seek: the durable consumer starts from the committed position and replays the missing event window atomically with the state reconstruction.
A cross-region disaster-recovery subscriber that mirrors events to a secondary site: the durable subscription in the secondary region receives every event from the primary's topic, with a DLQ holding any events that fail cross-region delivery for manual retry.
A JMS topic consumer that must receive publications made while it is offline: the client reconnects with the same client identifier and durable subscription name, and the provider retains messages until acknowledgement, expiry, or unsubscribe.
An MQTT 3.1.1 device gateway that reconnects with the same client identifier and CleanSession=0: the broker resumes the stored session and queues matching QoS 1/2 publications for delivery after the link returns.
A NATS JetStream billing worker that restarts after an outage: it binds to the same durable consumer name and explicit-acks each message, so the server resumes its acknowledgement floor and redelivers unacknowledged work.
An Azure Service Bus fan-out topology: topic subscriptions are durable by default and each subscription stores its own copy of matching messages, so a receiver that reconnects later still drains its backlog; client-affine durable subscriptions bind the durable state to a stable client id.
A high-throughput replay consumer on RabbitMQ Streams: the consumer attaches with a stable tracking reference (name) and periodically stores its offset server-side, so a restart resumes from the last stored offset instead of re-reading the whole stream.
An event-sourced system on Google Cloud Pub/Sub that must reprocess history after a bug fix: the subscription enables acknowledged-message retention (default window 7 days, up to 31) and is seeked back to a past timestamp or snapshot to replay already-acked messages.

recursive-descent-parser
recursive descent
recursive descent parsing
Parse a small grammar by translating every rule directly into a function that consumes the tokens the rule matches and calls the functions of the rules it references, so the parser's control flow is the grammar itself and stays readable, debuggable and free of a code-generation step.
A hand-written parser is the only option - no generator in the toolchain, or the grammar is a small DSL - yet the grammar is not a flat token sequence: alternatives must be chosen from lookahead, repetition must become a loop, and the natural grammar for expressions is left-recursive, which a top-down parser cannot translate directly. Without a disciplined mapping from rules to functions the parser degenerates into ad-hoc index arithmetic and exception-driven backtracking, and errors end up without positions.
Front ends for small languages, DSLs, query/filter/rule grammars, configuration and protocol formats, and the parsing layer of compilers and interpreters that want no code-generation step. It applies when a lexer or token stream already exists (or is cheap to write), the grammar is small to medium and reasonably LL-friendly or rewritable into LL form, and the team values readable, step-debuggable, position-precise parsing over generated tables.
Front ends for small languages, DSLs and configuration formats (filter expressions, rule engines, policy languages, template syntaxes) where a generator and its build integration would be overkill.
Expression and statement parsing in single-pass compilers and interpreters that emit bytecode or IR while parsing, as in Crafting Interpreters' Lox.
Tooling for a grammar you own - formatters, linters, syntax highlighters, language servers - where error tolerance, multiple diagnostics and exact positions matter more than raw throughput.
Protocol and wire-format decoding with a small fixed grammar, where errors must carry byte offsets and malformed input must be rejected deterministically.
Context-dependent or indentation-sensitive syntaxes (templates with interpolation, layout-based blocks, configuration with embedded expressions) that a generated lexer handles poorly.
Codebases that must not carry generated code: security-reviewed, vendored or cross-compiled projects where an ordinary source file beats a build-time generator.
Clang's C-family front end uses a unified hand-built recursive-descent parser for C, C++, Objective-C and Objective-C++, pairing rule-oriented control flow with production-quality diagnostics.
The Go standard library's go/parser is a production recursive-descent parser for Go source, with explicit parser state, nesting-depth guards and error recovery.
rustc_parse is the Rust compiler's recursive-descent parser module, showing how a hand-written parser can scale to macros, recovery modes and detailed token/state handling.
Lua's reference implementation compiles with lparser.c, a single-pass recursive-descent parser that emits bytecode opcodes while reducing expressions instead of building a syntax tree, with precedence handled by parsing levels.

state-colocation
colocated state
colocation
Keep each piece of presentation state in the component closest to where it is used — down to the single component that owns and reads it — instead of hoisting it to a common ancestor or a global store, so that a change touches only the smallest part of the view that can observe it.
